title: Pearl-Cohn announcer Catfish is James Brown of high school football
description: Orlando 'Catfish' Pender Jr. has been announcing football games at Pearl-Cohn High since the 1990s.
fullText:
Editor's note: The Tennessean is running a season-long, all-access series about the Pearl-Cohn football program. To follow along with the project, please 

Catfish will not, does not, cannot sit down.

Are you kidding? Catfish is all movement.

Orlando "Catfish" Pender Jr. is 82, born during World War II, raised in a family of share croppers in "North Crackalackin," he says.

"That's North Carolina," he explains with a wink.

Dressed all in Firebird red except for the black sneakers that never stop. There is a chair, right there, in the announcer's booth at Pearl-Cohn High School. But that chair might as well be his grave. Catfish will sit when he's dead.

Instead, the Pearl-Cohn stadium announcer for more than three decades bops around the booth, smacking the wall on a bad play, leaping to celebrate a touchdown, lunging to slap high fives with the scoreboard operator.

You've never heard a stadium announcer like Catfish.

"Get that fire started," he growls at the defense. "The fire has started. Let it buuuurrrrrnnnnn."

He's singing, dancing, smiling ... disappointed, depressed, mumbling ... the entire game, depending on the success or failure of his beloved Pearl-Cohn Firebirds.

Catfish says he announces football games like James Brown, the energetic belter of songs back in the day. All sweat, grunts and gyrations.

Catfish holds the microphone to his chest and begins a slow rumble.

"Come on ... Come on ... Come on ... Pearl-Cohn kickoff team. STAY IN YOUR LANE." He delivers that last line in the high baritone range.

And oh goodness if somebody fumbles, especially if that fumble is recovered by the Firebirds, Catfish breaks into a scream that sounds like someone set off fireworks in a thunderstorm.

"Fumblerooski is my favorite," Catfish says in a calmer moment.

There are other Catfish signature vocal gems. For the last two seasons, the Firebirds quarterback has been L.J. Funk, who appears to have been put on this earth just so Catfish, upon the completing of a Funk touchdown pass, can break into song.

"We want the Funk, gotta have that Funk," he sings like George Clinton sang in the disco days as the Pearl-Cohn crowd goes wild. Catfish dances around the booth like he's just won at karaoke night.

There is a church choir in his background, as you might guess, and encounters with Chuck Berry, Janis Joplin, Jimi Hendrix and other music icons.

Catfish met The Tennessean on a rainy Wednesday afternoon, telling his life story while he paced the floor of his home in North Nashville, the one with the "million dollar view" of downtown. Standing on his front porch, he can see the AT&T (Batman) Building.

He said the place was overgrown with weeds so high no one could see the "For Sale" sign when he bought it.

He owns "Catfish Moving Company," with four trucks and 12 employees. He's been married twice and is currently single. He has five children, 15 grandchildren and eight great-grandchildren.

And he's got songs. He points to his back room, a man cave, of sorts, where he keeps his songs, awards and pictures that go way back.

"I've got 250 songs," he says, most are gospel tunes. "I've got four songs in my head right now. 'I'm a soldier in the Army of the Lord.'"

You wouldn't know it by watching this happy blur of a man. But he has had to lean on his religion in recent years. Since the one tragic moment that stopped Catfish from moving.

The moment from which he is just now recovering.

Catfish bends at the waist, arms dangling in front of him. He's standing in his living room, reenacting the story that got him his nickname.

He had 11 siblings, and when you grow up on a tobacco, corn, cotton and barley farm in Wilson, North Carolina, you are responsible to bring home something for dinner. At first, he tried a homemade fishing pole with a bent safety pin as a hook. But he didn't have a cork to make the hook float, so he scrapped that idea.

That's why he's bent over in his living room, mimicking his movements as a child. Arms dangling in a stream, he would wait motionless until he could grab a catfish with his bare hands.

"You didn't come home empty handed," he said.

Just about as long as he can remember, he's been Catfish.

He played high school football, but he was 

It was 1963 when a 19-year-old Catfish went to Philadelphia to see the big city. That's when he said he heard the words, "Go in the service now." He said it was the voice of God.

Think about the timing. Catfish joined the Marines just before the buildup in Vietnam. He said he became a chauffeur. His job took him to Naples, Nice, Palermo, Istanbul, Beruit. "I went to Greece," he said. "I'm walking in the paths of Plato and Socrates."

"If I would have gone to Vietnam, I would be dead," he said.

He said he ended his service in 1967 after a year in the Military Police in Quantico, Virginia.

In the 1960s and '70s, he found himself bouncing around America. In New York City's Greenwich Village, he formed "The King Biscuit Blues Band" and he covered Muddy Waters songs. He said he was on the circuit with Hendrix, Joplin and Otis Redding.

In San Francisco, he formed a new band "The New Wave."

"I was the Black Paul McCartney," he said.

He tried LSD once. He said his eyes became kaleidoscopes, and he sat still. "I couldn't move," he said.

It was the fear of what drugs might do to him, and the deaths of Jimi, Janis and Jim Morrison that convinced him to settle down.

Catfish chose Nashville as the place to raise his family. There was Jaqueline, Jalonda, Orlando III, Apryll and Briana.

Nashville, he knew, was a good place to play gospel music. He joined the Born Again Church on West Trinity Lane and sang in the choir.

That choir was a powerhouse. They made a live album featuring gospel star CeCe Winans with other stars like Israel Houghton, Desmond Pringle, Steve Crawford and Da'dra Greathouse.

And Orlando "Catfish" Pender Jr.

The album was nominated for a Grammy in 2004.

As he talks, he has pride in his eyes.

It just so happened that the Born Again Church meetings were in the Pearl-Cohn High School auditorium.

At first, Catfish volunteered to be a sideline videographer for the Firebirds football team.

Then he became the mascot. He was in his 50s, but there was Catfish jumping around the sideline in a bird hat with red wings.

"I fell in love with Pearl-Cohn," he said. "And yes, I had feathers."

He said coach Maurice Fitzgerald loved his voice, so he asked Catfish to be the public address announcer.

Catfish brought an energy to the booth that may be unfamiliar to fans who only hear monotone "First and 10" from most stadium announcers.

"I gotta do me," Catfish said. He loves when Pearl-Cohn whips an opponent, and still the opposing fans thank him for the energy he brings.

"The gift I have is my voice," he said. "I'm not saying something that's stale ... Elvis wanted to be the best. James Brown wanted to be the best. I want to be the best at something."

Pearl-Cohn football statistician Calvin Peters said Catfish brings the entertainment.

"He means the world to Pearl-Cohn," Peters said. "He brings a certain flair like no one else. His sayings and quotes are legendary."

Catfish stops when he talks about Janaye.

His granddaughter was in the Pearl-Cohn marching band, another in the long line of his relatives raised on Firebird football. She played the piccolo, following in the footsteps of her mother Jalonda, who played the clarinet.

Janaye was 31 in 2023 when she died due to a fentanyl overdose.

"I wasn't prepared for it," Orlando Pender Jr. says.

The happiest man you will ever meet didn't know how to deal with it.

"I went through denial, grief and torment," he said. "My heart was finally broken."

As football season begins again, he said Catfish has come back.

"He has sustained his spirit," said Pearl-Cohn head football coach Tony Brunetti. "He has a strong mind, a strong soul."

A smile appears on Catfish's face.

"I feel invincible," he says. "But I am not."

title: Jadarian Price makes his NFL debut today. A former teammate expects big things
description: Jadarian Price is making his NFL debut in the Seahawks' season opener against the Patriots. His former teammate is bullish about his NFL potential.
fullText:
Jadarian Price is looking to prove the Seattle Seahawks right for making him the first running back the team has selected in the first round of the NFL draft since Rashaad Penny in 2018.

At least one of Price's former teammates believes he will be able to find high-level success in the NFL.

Jeremiyah Love, who played with Price during their time together at Notre Dame, is bullish about his former counterpart's NFL prospects, as he told USA TODAY Sports in an April interview as part of his partnership with New Balance.

"I tell everybody this. I feel like JD can do everything I can do, if not more," Love said, referring to Price by his nickname.

Love expressed confidence in Price's skills as a runner, pass-catcher and blocker. He also referred to the 22-year-old as the best return man in the country, saying that Price returns kicks "way better than me."

That's why the No. 3 overall selection in the 2026 NFL Draft believes his first-round counterpart will be able to handle all that's required of an NFL running back, like himself.

"JD is a back that can do everything," Love said. "You give him a hole, he's gonna take that hole and he's gonna take it all the way to the house. JD's that type of back."

The Seahawks are certainly banking on that being the case. They drafted Price, in part, to help replace departed Super Bowl 60 MVP Kenneth Walker III, who signed with the Kansas City Chiefs in free agency.

Meanwhile, Walker's foil, Zach Charbonnet, is coming off a torn ACL and will miss at least the first four games of the season while on the physically unable to perform (PUP) list.

That should give Price an early chance to prove his former teammate turned division rival right and stake a claim to Seattle's top running back role for the foreseeable future.

Here's more to know about Price as he makes his NFL debut during the Seahawks' season opener against the New England Patriots.

Price played three college seasons at Notre Dame but largely played second fiddle to Love. During his final season, Price logged 113 carries for 674 yards and 11 touchdowns while adding 87 yards and two touchdowns on six catches. He also posted two kick return touchdowns on 12 return attempts with an FBS-best average of 37.5 yards per return.

Below is a full look at Price's stats across his three seasons with the Fighting Irish:

Price's strong performance helped convince the Seahawks to select him with the 32nd overall pick in the 2026 NFL Draft. He was the final pick of the first round while he and Love became the first pair of college teammates to be the top two running backs selected across any draft in NFL history.

The Seahawks opted not to play Price during the preseason. Neither he nor projected backup George Holani logged any carries as Seattle looked to keep both fresh for the start of the season amid Charbonnet's injury.

Price is expected to be the lead back in Seattle's offense to open the season.

That said, it's worth noting that the Seahawks' official website actually lists Holani ahead of him on the depth chart for now. It isn't clear whether that is a product of Price not playing the preseason or if it is a reflection of the veteran being slightly ahead of the rookie entering the season.

Seattle currently has three running backs on the 53-man roster. Here's a look at the projected pecking order within that room to open the season:

Price and Holani could see a relatively even workload split early in the season. The situation could be similar to those faced by Jahmyr Gibbs and Bijan Robinson as rookies in 2023, when Gibbs shared touches with David Montgomery and Robinson did the same with Tyler Allgeier.

Whenever Charbonnet returns, he will be expected to overtake Holani in the complementary role alongside Price.

The Seahawks also have Velus Jones Jr. and Jacardia Wright on the practice squad. Both are candidates to be called up to add backfield and special teams depth, if necessary.

title: Cleveland Browns predictions for entire 2026 NFL season
description: The Browns kick off the season Sept. 13 against the Jacksonville Jaguars. So how will the season play out for them? We take a guaess here.
fullText:
BEREA ― Time to break out the crystal ball. So if you've got any problems with what follows, blame the sphere, not the writer.

The day the Browns' 2026 schedule came out, we made a knee-jerk reaction win-loss prediction on how the season would play out. The result we ended up with was a 5-12 record.

Well, four months later, with OTAs and minicamp and training camp and preseason games all having been completed to add context, we're back here to take a swing at guessing the way the season will go. This time, we're even going to throw in scores that are sure to be nowhere near what they ultimately end up being.

Well, scared money don't make any money. So let's try this again to see how the 2026 Browns season plays out.

Location, time: Everbank Stadium, 1 p.m. ET

About the game: Deshaun Watson starting for the first time since mid-October 2024. A rookie left tackle who's only played 30-some preseason game snaps in the NFL having to face two-time Pro Bowler Josh Hines-Allen in his first regular-season game. All of that against a Jaguars offense that will be in the second season under coach Liam Coen. Not necessarily the recipe for success.

Score prediction: Jaguars 30, Browns 17

Location, time: Raymond James Stadium, 1 p.m. ET

About the game: Baker Mayfield's going to have a chip on his shoulder the size of a boulder for this game. The Florida heat is going to be a factor for the second week in a row. It's a little closer, but it's still 0-2.

Score prediction: Buccaneers 24, Browns 21

Location, time: Huntington Bank Field, 1 p.m. ET

About the game: It's tempting to say this is when Shedeur Sanders makes his first start, but after two games seems a tad quick to pull the cord. This is a game where the defense gives the Browns a chance. A chance, not a win.

Score prediction: Panthers 21, Browns 20

Location, time: Huntington Bank Field, 8:20 p.m. ET

About the game: You don't make a quarterback change on the short week. Both of these teams may already want to do that by this point. The Browns ride their defense, their Thursday night success and their recent dominance over the Steelers in Cleveland to their first win.

Score prediction: Browns 24, Steelers 17

Location, time: MetLife Stadium, 1 p.m. ET

About the game: Well, can you change your starting quarterback off your first win of the season? Especially when you're going on the road to face the Jets? No, but you can after you lose to the Jets for the second time in as many years.

Score prediction: Jets 17, Browns 14

Location, time: Huntington Bank Field, 1 p.m. ET

About the game: Much like he did a year ago against the Ravens, Sanders makes a hero's debut, only this time as the starter. The Browns are going to catch one of either Baltimore or Cincinnati in Cleveland. Well, here's the one.

Score prediction: Browns 28, Ravens 27

Location, time: Nissan Stadium, 1 p.m. ET

About the game: Shedeur Sanders vs. Cam Ward Part II. This time, it's Sanders who prevails. That makes it two in a row, which is what they call a "winning streak."

Score prediction: Browns 35, Titans 28

Location, time: Acrisure Stadium, 1 p.m. ET

About the game: Nothing brings a Cleveland Browns win streak to a end quicker than a trip to Pittsburgh. Not picking a Browns win there until they actually prove they can win a game that's not being played in an empty stadium there.

Score prediction: Steelers 24, Browns 13

Location, time: Caesars Superdome, 1 p.m. ET

About the game: Another road game that could go any number of ways, just because there are any number of ways the Saints' season could go. Maybe the Browns catch the Superdome crowd a tad hung over from LSU playing Alabama the night before. Or, perhaps the Browns catch Tyler Shough continuing to rise.

Score prediction: Saints 31, Browns 21

Location, time: Huntington Bank Field, 1 p.m. ET

About the game: Remembered what the Browns defense looked like with Myles Garrett? That's what the Texans defense looks like with Will Anderson.

Score prediction: Texans 28, Browns 10

About the game: If the math is right, the Browns hit the bye week with a 3-7 record by this prediction.

Score prediction: Only prediction is a much-needed break for all involved.

About the game: If the Browns didn't have Myles Garrett last year, there's a better than average chance Fernando Mendoza is a Cleveland Brown right now. Instead, he's on the Raiders, but it's not 100% certain he'll be starting by this point.

Score prediction: Browns 28, Raiders 20

Location, time: Huntington Bank Field, 1 p.m. ET

About the game: Already gave the Browns their one home win over either Baltimore or Cincinnati. If Garrett was still here, this one might feel 

Score prediction: Bengals 38, Browns 21

Location, time: Huntington Bank Field, 1 p.m. ET

About the game: Kevin Stefanski won a lot of games in this stadium when he was on the home sideline. Feels like he's going to win another one, only on the other sideline.

Score prediction: Falcons 24, Browns 22

Location, time: MetLife Stadium, 1 p.m. ET

About the game: Could this potentially be the Browns against yet another former quarterback of theirs? It seems doubtful that Jaxson Dart will still be healthy by this point of the season, which means it's going to be Jameis Winston time for the Giants. Cleveland goes 0-2 against the New York teams.

title: John Cominsky details NFL retirement, new project with HOF honors next
description: Ex-Detroit Lions defensive lineman John Cominsky will be inducted into the Summit County Sports Hall of Fame and the Barberton Sports HOF this fall.
fullText:
John Cominsky has redirected the energy he needed to ascend from an underdog at Barberton High School to a starter on an NFL playoff team, using his commitment and passion to promote health education after retiring as a defensive lineman in March 2025.

Cominsky recently told the Beacon Journal he suffered "three significant" concussions as a member of the Detroit Lions in 2023. Those injuries contributed to him leaving the NFL and shifting more of his attention to assisting communities in Northeast Ohio through his Cominsky Family Foundation.

For the past six months, Cominsky has been making weekly visits to a drug and alcohol treatment center in Massillon, where he works with patients on breathing techniques and light exercise.

"It empowers an individual to see, 'Hey, if I move and breathe, I can flush this thought, I can get back to center, I can start my day off right and I can change my attitude,'" said Cominsky, who lives in Hinckley.

Watch Ohio High School Football Live on NFHS Network all year

In the meantime, Cominsky's supporters are honoring him for his on-field achievements. He will be inducted into the Summit County Sports Hall of Fame on Oct. 6 and the Barberton Sports Hall of Fame on Nov. 25.

The 30-year-old Cominsky said he's eager to celebrate his fellow inductees and express gratitude to his backers.

"I'm just proud to represent all those people that invested in me," he said.

More local sports: Summit County Sports Hall of Fame's new class has Akron Zips greats and former NFL players

Cominsky transformed from a lightly recruited jack-of-all-trades Barberton football player who quarterbacked the Magics as a senior to a 285-pound defensive end at Division II University of Charleston in West Virginia.

Eating became a job for Cominsky in college as he gained about 70 pounds and evolved into a dominant force in the trenches. He earned All-America status and the Mountain East Conference Defensive Player of the Year award en route to becoming the first Charleston player to be drafted in 68 years when the Atlanta Falcons chose him in the fourth round (No. 135 overall) in 2019.

Cominsky played five seasons in the NFL (three with the Falcons and two with the Lions) and started 20 of the 57 regular-season games in which he appeared, compiling 107 tackles, with 11 for loss and 7.5 sacks, 25 quarterback hits, a forced fumble, a fumble recovery and six passes defensed. In Cominsky's final season, he started 11 of 17 regular-season games and all three playoff games for the 2023 Lions while they made a run to the NFC championship game.

As a member of the Summit County Sports Hall of Fame's board of directors and the president of the Barberton Sports Hall of Fame, Rob Culbertson championed Cominsky's candidacy for his upcoming inductions. Culbertson was a teacher, athletic trainer and athletic director at Barberton during Cominsky's high school years.

"It is just mind-boggling that he was able to take his body and his mind and set a course for himself, set goals, and then he worked his tail off, did as his coaches told him to do, gained the weight and, lo and behold, he was able to get drafted," Culbertson said. "… He is the epitome of what the Barberton community is all about."

Cominsky hasn't forgotten his roots. He and his wife, Brittany, a fellow Barberton native, run the Cominsky Family Foundation. They have held a free youth football camp at Barberton High School for years, aided local businesses, given kids backpacks filled with non-perishable food items and delivered turkeys to pantries for Thanksgiving.

"We also are working with other organizations trying to bolster the out-of-school-time youth experience in Barberton year-round," John Cominsky said.

More John Cominsky: 'It's once in a lifetime': Barberton native helps 2023 Lions reach NFC title game

Meanwhile, health education is at the forefront of Cominsky's plans. A separate business venture in Massillon made him aware of the OVP Health Recovery Center, the drug and alcohol treatment facility where he encourages patients to breathe and move.

Cominsky calls the sessions he hosts "teatime." As an icebreaker of sorts, he wheels in a cart with hot water, tea bags and honey, offering beverages to patients who may be guarded.

"The tea is just this warm welcome," Cominsky said.

The meetings typically last for a half hour to an hour.

"I believe in meditation. I believe in breathing techniques," Cominsky said. "But when you come in with that as your spearhead, people will reject you.

"I go in and we just do basic movement and breath work. I introduce myself, 'Hey, I'm John. I believe moving and breathing is good for you. Who wants to join me?'

"It gives these people an opportunity to see the power of simple habits and routine and just how much discipline, although people see it as restricting freedom, it actually creates freedom."

About 15 to 20 people attend "teatime" each week in Massillon, Cominsky said. He has also dabbled in events with IBF Addiction Recovery in Akron.

"I've kind of wiggled my way into drug recovery without being a former addict myself, which is pretty unlikely," Cominsky said. "Even the higher-up leaders [at rehabilitation centers], a lot of them have fought addiction themselves, and so I feel grateful to have the conviction to serve this community without the history."

Cominsky said he has a desire for people to be healthy, and he wants them to prioritize health. He thought about becoming a doctor — or a pursuing another profession in the medical field — as a biology and chemistry major at Charleston. He said his enthusiasm for health and wellness would exist even if his football career had not ended the way it did, with concerns about the concussions he has endured.

"But it shines a little bit more light on it because I kind of have these lingering issues," Cominsky said. "In boxing, they call it punch-drunk. It's kind of like you have half a beer in you all the time. It's kind of like a slight vertigo. It's something I've grown used to, and it has improved.

"I have a true a gauge [for inflammation in my body] because my symptoms flare up. It's directly related to poor habits. It's directly related to if I have bad sleep, if I eat bad, if I'm dehydrated. All these things flare up."

Cominsky also suffered a torn medial collateral ligament and cartilage damage in his right knee early in the Lions' 2024 training camp. He underwent surgery and never played again in the NFL.

"I had a lot of cartilage that kind of got chipped out," he said, "almost like a golf divot right under my kneecap, and that's what was giving me most of the issues.

"I'm still dealing with things in my knee. I have a lot of cartilage missing, and it really took a while to bounce back, probably a full two years after the injury to feel 90%."

Cominsky said a silver lining is the knee injury "probably saved my brain a little bit" by sidelining him for the entire 2024 season.

As Cominsky reflected on his NFL career in 2024, he concluded the concussions from the previous year had affected his performance on the field.

"I'm looking at my game film, and I'm just watching a little bit of hesitancy," Cominsky said. "My edge when I played was that I played with my hair on fire, and I had no remorse for anything, anybody, my own body, whatever.

"I started to see myself make what they call in the NFL 'business decisions.' There's a play. The guy's probably going to go down. Just peel away. You don't have to stick your nose in there. So, I started to see these signs of like, 'Oh, buddy. Hey, you're losing your edge a little bit.'"

Of course, Cominsky thought about his future with his family, too. In 2022, he and Brittany had their first child, now 4-year-old daughter Emersyn. In 2024, Brittany became pregnant with the couple's now 1-year-old son, Wren.

"Between my family developing and the concussions that I had, I just didn't have the fire that was required of me," Cominsky said. "… I just couldn't do it, and so I was very fortunate to be able to walk away.

"It was just too many concussions, and I lost my fire. There's guys out there with fire times a hundred, and you don't want to be on the same field as somebody who is all in when you're not 100% in. So, it was time."

Cominsky turned to a new chapter, and he plans to write many more.

"I'm pretty set on this health education piece and bringing that to all people, including vulnerable populations," he said.

The Summit County Sport Hall of Fame's 68th induction ceremony and banquet will be held on Tuesday, Oct. 6, at Annunciation Greek Orthodox Church, 129 S. Union St., Akron. Doors are scheduled to open at 5:15 p.m. A social/cocktail hour is slated to run from 5:30-6:30 p.m. The program and dinner are set to start at 6:30 p.m.

In addition to Cominsky, this year's SCSHOF inductees are James Eberwine (rifle), Doran Grant (football), John Groce (basketball coach), Jeff Howard (cross country and track and field coach), Whitney Mercilus (football), Hope Murphy (cross country and track) and Rachel Tecca-Fleming (basketball).

title: Utd goal v Ipswich backed by league panel despite Maguire handball
description: The decision to allow a Manchester United goal against Ipswich after a handball by Harry Maguire has been backed by the Premier League’s Key Match Incidents (KMI) Panel – though one panellist felt the handball was deliberate. The ball appeared to come off Maguire’s hand as he controlled it just outside the penalty area during the match on August 30.
fullText:
The decision to allow a Manchester United goal against Ipswich after a handball by Harry Maguire has been backed by the Premier League's Key Match Incidents (KMI) Panel – though one panellist felt the handball was deliberate.

The ball appeared to come off Maguire's hand as he controlled it just outside the penalty area during the match on August 30. He then unleashed a shot, which was going wide before being deflected in by Jacob Greaves in United's 5-2 win.

The handball was deemed to be accidental by both referee Craig Pawson and VAR Jarred Gillett, and because Maguire's shot did not go in directly, that meant the goal was allowed to stand.

The KMI Panel is an independent group comprised of three former players or coaches, one Premier League representative and one from officiating body Pro Ref. Panel findings on key incidents in every game-week are being published this season for the first time.

The panel said on Wednesday: "Maguire's arms are within his bodyline, meaning that the contact with his right arm was accidental and not a punishable handball offence given that Maguire was not the goal scorer.

"The shot was clearly off-target and then deflected in via the defender for a clear own goal. The panel supported the referee's call to award the goal, 4:1, with one panellist considering the handball to be deliberate."

On the day of the match, the Premier League's Match Centre account on X posted: "The referee's call of goal for Manchester United was checked and confirmed by VAR – with it deemed that Maguire was not the immediate goalscorer after an accidental handball."

The same post also quoted the VAR: "It's an own goal and the accidental handball is not punishable, so we recommend you award the goal."

title: What Lane Kiffin book reveals about Ole Miss departure, wanting Trinidad Chambliss at LSU
description: The Clarion Ledger got a review copy of "Lane Being Lane," John Talty's book about former Ole Miss coach Lane Kiffin now at LSU.
fullText:
OXFORD — A new book attempts to answer the Lane Kiffin question Ole Miss football fans asked repeatedly during his dramatic departure last year.

"Lane Being Lane" is the third college football book from John Talty, who was a Clarion Ledger recruiting writer from 2012-14. It will release Sept. 15, shortly before Kiffin and LSU are scheduled to return to Oxford in Week 3 for a game against Ole Miss on Sept. 19 (6:30 p.m., ABC).

Talty provided the Clarion Ledger with an advance copy. Kiffin did not participate directly in the book.

"I want to just dive super deep into who this guy is and why he does the things he does," Talty told the Clarion Ledger. "Like, how did he get here? Why does he do these things?"

The book presents a look at Kiffin's life, starting from his childhood and finishing after Kiffin went to LSU on Nov. 30, 2025. Fans will read a comprehensive recount of the bitter split between Kiffin and Ole Miss.

Right before Kiffin's departure, a source in the book likens Kiffin's behavior during a meeting with Ole Miss Athletic Director Keith Carter and Chancellor Glenn Boyce to that of a "kid having a temper tantrum." The meeting was about if Kiffin would be allowed to coach in the College Football Playoff. It was supposed to take 10 minutes. It lasted two hours.

"I think for the first time ever he finally heard Keith Carter say no," Ole Miss booster Smitty Smith says in the book.

The book details how Kiffin contacted sports attorney Tom Mars late in the 2025 season to fight for quarterback Trinidad Chambliss' eligibility. As time wore on and Kiffin left for LSU, Mars details how Kiffin asked for updates via text or calls several times per day.

"It was clear to me — it would be cleat to anyone except the village idiot — that he was hoping the appeal would be granted so he could bring Trinidad to LSU," Mars said.

Talty writes that, despite Kiffin's public support of his former team, Kiffin was "despondent" when Ole Miss beat Georgia in the College Football Playoff without him. Talty includes a story from an unnamed close friend of Kiffin's.

"It was killing him. He was texting us non-stop during the game. Sends me ... a picture of (Ole Miss running back) Kewan Lacy in an LSU uniform dunking on Ole Miss during the (expletive) game."

In the book, that friend later said Kiffin "lost his mind" when Lacy committed to return to Ole Miss. The book goes on to detail about how Kiffin egged on Clemson coach Dabo Swinney to report Ole Miss tampering for transfer linebacker Luke Ferrelli. Swinney has since denied it.

One of the book's themes is how polarizing Kiffin is.

"You could ask fifty guys about Lane and they would say he was an arrogant asshole," high school football teammate Casey Elder said in the book. "Fifty other guys would say, 'What a great guy.' He was cocky and confident but a good guy, I fell into that camp."

The book traces how a laundry list of revered figures have shaped Kiffin's career: His father Monte Kiffin, former USC coach Pete Carroll, former Alabama coach Nick Saban and agent Jimmy Sexton. There are also stories about little-known people who helped make Kiffin, including his high school football coach and childhood friends.

Kiffin's time as a mischievous high school football player is revisited, and his days as a young, sometimes brash assistant coach climbing the coach ladder at USC with Ed Orgeron and Steve Sarkisian. Kiffin's time as the head coach of the Oakland Raiders is, fittingly, just one chapter.

Ole Miss fans will find Talty's recount of Kiffin's six years in Oxford fascinating. There are highs, like the 2023 Chick-fil-A Peach Bowl win over Penn State (the final game Kiffin had with his father) and when Ole Miss beat Georgia on a rainy Oxford night in 2024.

There are also lows. It's not a gossipy book, but it doesn't shy away from Kiffin's off-the-field struggles. High-level Ole Miss boosters are interviewed. So is a licensed psychologist who specializes in sexual addiction, and a bar employee in Tuscaloosa, Alabama.

The book recounts when Kiffin, who did not have personal private plane usage in his first Ole Miss contract, grumbled about it. When an Ole Miss donor set him up with an $8 million King Air private plane, Kiffin reportedly sent some donors a text of a photo of himself in the plane describing it as a "piece of (expletive)."

When Ole Miss and LSU play, Kiffin's return will be a fascinating look at a hero-turned-villain in his old home. It will be the latest example of why Talty chose his tagline for the book: College football's Agent of Chaos.

"He's just had such a fascinating one of one coaching career," Talty said. "Like truly, no one else has had a coaching career like this guy."

title: Fantasy football cheat sheet: The risk of trusting Jeremiyah Love, Jadarian Price
description: Jeremiyah Love and Jadarian Price should blossom into fantasy football assets, but will they start hot? Our weekly cheat sheet breaks it down.
fullText:
Welcome to USA TODAY Sports' fantasy football cheat sheet column, where each week I'll provide you with plenty of tips, tricks and strategies about how to win your fantasy league and also regale you with stories and lessons learned from my 16 years of playing fantasy football. For more fantasy advice, check out our new premium tools that can help you make start/sit decisions and figure out how best to attack the waiver wire.

It's finally here. The 2026 NFL season is starting on Wednesday, Sept. 9, with a Super Bowl 60 rematch between the New England Patriots and Seattle Seahawks.

As kickoff arrives, fantasy football managers will grow increasingly eager to get a glance at their new players in action. That will be particularly true for the rookies they placed their faith in as potential value picks and sleepers ahead of their NFL debuts.

Rookies certainly carry sky-high ceilings in fantasy football. Managers have been reminded of this by the star turns of talents like Ja'Marr Chase and, further back, Ezekiel Elliott, who became instant league-winners early in their careers.

Even so, trusting rookies can also be an early-season pitfall for fantasy managers. The reason for this is simple. While top-tier rookies are sometimes thrust into big roles out of the gate, like Chase and Elliott, more often they have to compete for playing time as they acclimate to the NFL.

Now, that's not to say fantasy managers can't trust a first-year player in Week 1. It's just important to know what to expect from them as they begin their respective NFL careers.

That can be the difference between enjoying a successful Week 1 and falling as flat as Max Bialystock does on his "Opening Night" in the musical adaptation of "The Producers."

Without further ado, let's dive right into those expectations as the 2026 NFL season begins.

Look, I know what you're going to say. You didn't draft Love or Price early to sit them on the bench early in the season. I get it, but it's still important to know what to expect from the talented Notre Dame products.

Love and Price should eventually emerge as three-down threats for their respective franchises, but the key word is eventually. Both running backs will face challenges getting playing time early in their careers, which could limit their ceilings.

In Seattle, Price is expected to share snaps with veteran George Holani to open the season. Many had hoped the Notre Dame product would earn a lion's share of the snaps with his expected foil, Zach Charbonnet, out at least four games while continuing to recover from a torn ACL. Instead, the Seahawks may try to ease the 22-year-old into action after he didn't earn a carry during the preseason.

The situation is a bit more complicated in Arizona. Love is expected to play in Week 1, but he is recovering from a high-ankle sprain. That injury interrupted his trajectory toward emerging as the clear-cut backfield leader with the Cardinals. Now, he seems far more likely to split carries with veteran Tyler Allgeier, which could limit his upside early in the season.

These situations are reminiscent of another cautionary tale fantasy managers – and yours truly – encountered in 2023. During his rookie season, Jahmyr Gibbs was an early-round pick whose explosive speed was expected to allow him to eventually emerge as the Detroit Lions' lead back and a viable RB1.

Gibbs flashed those skills, but he struggled to fully overtake David Montgomery. Across the first seven weeks of the season, Gibbs averaged a solid 75 total yards per game but only scored one touchdown in his five appearances, making him more of an inconsistent flex play.

Gibbs got more opportunities down the stretch of the season, and eventually worked his way into the RB1 conversation. However, by that point, many fantasy managers who trusted him as their RB2 and a top-three-round selection had fallen out of contention, leaving them to look ahead to future seasons.

The comparison isn't perfect. Montgomery is far more of a proven workhorse than either Allgeier or Holani. As such, one would expect the time-shares in Arizona and Seattle to eventually end, unlike the early days of the "Sonic and Knuckles" partnership in Detroit, especially if the upper-echelon talent of Love and Price can shine through early in the season.

Still, Love and Price look more like short-term boom-or-bust flex plays. It won't necessarily hurt fantasy managers to play either – the dearth of quality running back depth could easily allow each to emerge as a solid RB2, even in a down week – but they may not immediately produce at the clip many were hoping when they spent early-round selections on the Notre Dame duo.

If predicting the workloads of Love and Price is difficult, then figuring out what the top rookie receivers will do is next to impossible.

The issue with the receiver prospects isn't talent. Eight were top-50 selections in the 2026 NFL Draft, highlighting their talent and potential as long-term contributors at the NFL level.

Still, many face uncertain roles, while others are in unfavorable situations that could hurt their early productivity in the NFL.

Some examples of the former? New York Jets first-round pick Omar Cooper Jr. is listed as a backup on the team's depth chart, so it isn't clear whether he will earn a big role to open the season. The same is true of Pittsburgh Steelers second-round pick Germie Bernard, who finds himself behind DK Metcalf, Michael Pittman Jr. and Roman Wilson in Pittsburgh's projected pecking order.

Meanwhile, the Cleveland Browns' quarterback problems could limit KC Concepcion and Denzel Boston. New Orleans Saints first-round pick Jordyn Tyson is on IR with a hamstring injury, while the Tennessee Titans' No. 4 overall pick, Carnell Tate, needs to develop better chemistry with Cam Ward after failing to catch a pass during the preseason.

OK, that feels like a lot of negativity, and I don't mean to imply that none of these players will find success. But sometimes, fantasy managers need to be patient with their young talents. Yes, they have breakout potential, but it's best to sit them until fantasy managers see some of that in action during the regular season.

So, are there any rookie receivers to start in Week 1? I'd entertain the notion of Makai Lemon, who should see plenty of targets for a Philadelphia Eagles team replacing A.J. Brown, but De'Zhaun Stribling may be the safest pick to produce.

Stribling was viewed as a curious second-round choice, but he was a standout during the preseason, generating 11 catches for 109 yards across two games. He has a clear path toward targets in a 49ers offense that lost Ricky Pearsall for the season to a knee injury and may want to ease tight end George Kittle back in his return from a torn Achilles.

That should be enough to make Stribling a volume-based flex or WR3 to start his career, even in a tough matchup against the Los Angeles Rams in Australia.

Pointing out the obvious, there aren't any rookie QBs worth rostering at present in non-dynasty leagues. That is unlikely to change until Fernando Mendoza sees the field for the Las Vegas Raiders, though Carson Beck can also be monitored in deeper leagues should Jacoby Brissett struggle for the Cardinals.

But even if either rookie starts, he isn't guaranteed to emerge as even a streamer given the depth and talent among the veteran quarterbacks this year.

Tight end is a bit more interesting since teams selected a lot of players at the position in 2026. Still, the only one with potential fantasy value is Kenyon Sadiq, another first-round pick of the Jets, and even he might not be ready to contribute early in his career.

So, don't waste too much time trying to hunt for upside at these positions. Feel free to stash Sadiq or monitor him on waivers, but generally speaking, any and all rookie assessment should be focused on running backs and wide receivers to open the 2026 season.

It's never too early to look ahead to the waiver wire. These players don't necessarily need to be picked up before NFL Week 1, but keep an eye on them as potential FAAB spend-ups and waiver targets once the first week of action wraps up.

All roster percentages via Yahoo Fantasy.

QB Malik Willis, Dolphins (41% rostered). Willis is an accurate quarterback with elite mobility playing for a Dolphins team that figures to be frequently trailing. His rushing upside alone will make him a quality week-to-week streamer, and playing for Miami should unlock plenty of garbage-time scoring opportunities for him.

RB Tyler Allgeier, Cardinals (48% rostered). We already talked about Love's ankle injury and the potential for him to split touches with Allgeier. The 26-year-old served as a goal-line vulture behind Bijan Robinson, so don't be surprised if he takes some scores away from Love early in the season and emerges as a decent flex play.

RB Jonah Coleman, Broncos (34% rostered). Coleman is behind J.K. Dobbins and RJ Harvey on Denver's depth chart, but Dobbins is oft-injured while Harvey averaged just 3.7 yards per carry as a rookie. Coleman has elite contact balance and could eventually emerge as a key part of the Broncos' backfield rotation, if given the opportunity.

WR Malachi Fields, Giants (6% rostered). Fields seemingly won the battle for the Giants' No. 2 receiver job during the preseason. The third-round rookie has a massive, 64-, 222-pound frame and should be a great contested catch and red-zone weapon, giving him touchdown upside across fantasy formats.

WR Chris Bell, Dolphins (5% rostered). Bell was viewed as a potential first-round talent in the 2026 NFL Draft before suffering a torn ACL. He is working his way back into game shape but could eventually emerge as Miami's No. 1 receiver. Like Willis, he should benefit from playing in garbage time, so he's worth an upside swing.

title: Jeremiah Smith has been quiet against Texas. Can Ohio State get him going in rematch?
description: Some incredible numbers show how much Texas has limited Ohio State star wide receiver Jeremiah Smith in the past. Will that continue in 2026?
fullText:
Jeremiah Smith has presented opponents with matchup nightmares since arriving at Ohio State, overwhelming defensive backs with his size and speed.

But in each of the past two years, Texas has kept him in check.

Between the 2025 season opener and the teams' earlier meeting in the College Football Playoff semifinals, Smith has combined for just seven receptions for 46 yards.

The modest production looms large ahead of their rematch in Austin on Sept. 12, as the Buckeyes look for ways to maximize the impact of their superstar receiver, arguably the best player in college football.

"It's no mystery that when the ball is in his hands, good things happen," Ohio State coach Ryan Day said.

While Day said the Buckeyes would work to make sure Smith is a major factor against the Longhorns, he has hardly been an afterthought in previous game plans. Texas has just sold out to stop him.

The Longhorns devoted significant attention to Smith in both games, using deep zone coverages to keep him from beating them over the top.

When they held Smith to one catch for 3 yards in the playoff semifinals, safety Michael Taaffe floated toward his side of the field to help in coverage.

Smith has not caught a pass deeper than 7 yards downfield against the Longhorns. Even as quarterback Julian Sayin found Smith touches last season, it was largely a mix of screens, curls and other short routes to the flats. The average depth of Smith's 10 targets was a mere 3.7 yards, according to Pro Football Focus.

Smith also had two uncharacteristic drops against Texas last season, and he was still in the early stages of building chemistry with Sayin, who was in his debut as Ohio State's starting quarterback.

"There were opportunities where I could have taken the ball toward him," Sayin said. "I wouldn't say they limited him in any aspect."

The most glaring instance was on a fourth-and-1 at midfield on the Buckeyes' opening drive. Sayin found tight end Max Klare toward the sideline, but Smith was open streaking downfield, having burst through a seam. Klare dropped the pass. One to Smith might have produced a touchdown.

Sayin and Smith were on the same page when the Buckeyes opened their season last weekend with a 56-3 win over Ball State. Smith caught eight passes for 151 yards and two touchdowns in the first half alone. He rested in the second half as the game grew lopsided, with Ohio State anticipating this week's trip to Texas for a top-five matchup.

It remains to be seen how much Texas will follow the same approach after hiring Will Muschamp as defensive coordinator to replace Pete Kwiatkowski, who was fired by coach Steve Sarkisian in December after five seasons with the Longhorns.

Muschamp has not been a primary defensive coordinator since he was at Auburn in 2015, adding a new variable to the series with the uncertainty over how the Longhorns will evolve under his direction. The unknown has Day's attention, as he acknowledged the limits to their pregame preparations. The Buckeyes will likely need to adjust after the ball is snapped.

"But we know that there will be a plan to stop Jeremiah," Day said, "try to identify what that is and then have the plans in place for what that looks like."

Day said Sayin will have a significant role in helping to identify Texas' tendencies in game, a situation in which his year of starting experience could pay dividends.

"He's got to recognize what's going on and respond from there," Day said. "All those things are part of our conversation as we put our game plan together."

For as much as Texas has contained Smith, it has not been Ohio State's undoing. The Buckeyes won both meetings.

The Longhorns' devotion to Smith allowed Carnell Tate to emerge as a weapon. Tate was the Buckeyes' leading receiver in both games, combining for nine catches for 136 yards and a touchdown.

Tate's 40-yard scoring haul in last year's 14-7 win gave the Buckeyes a commanding lead early in the fourth quarter.

"What makes a great player great is he makes everybody on the field better," Day said, "and certainly Jeremiah does that."

With Tate having left for the NFL, the Buckeyes have a new cast of receivers poised to benefit from the attention devoted to Smith, a group led by UTSA transfer Devin McCuin and returning slot receiver Brandon Inniss.

Ohio State defensive end Kenyatta Jackson Jr. said he has never seen an opponent contain Smith to this degree. Even when they were high school teammates years earlier at Chaminade-Madonna in Hollywood, Florida, Smith dominated defenses.

"Every team we went against, he put 150-plus on them," Jackson said.

But Jackson said Smith has handled the frustrations against Texas well.

"He wants to make plays for sure," Jackson said, "but as long as the team wins, he's OK with it. That's the type of person he is."

Labeling Smith "arguably the best player in college football," Texas coach Steve Sarkisian spoke at length to the media on Sept. 7 about the Ohio State wide receiver.

"I think, one, he garners your attention and he deserves our attention," Sarkisian said. "... The challenge is, with him, it's the size, speed, catch radius. He's a big, physical guy who can cover a lot of ground in a short amount of time. It doesn't always look like it, but it almost feels like it. You can feel his presence on the field.

"... This guy looks like Julio Jones. This guy looks like A.J. Brown physically. He can cover ground and then, because he's so strong, 50-50 catches are difficult with him. You have to have a plan. But I think like anything when you have a plan against somebody like him, you can't just throw all fastballs. As good as a fastball as you have, if that's all you got, sooner or later you're gonna hit it. We've got to be able to mix our pitches up in how we defend him and how we defend the scheme."

Joey Kaufman covers Ohio State football for The Columbus Dispatch. Email him at jkaufman@dispatch.com and follow him on @joeyrkaufman on X.

Staff reporter Dan Aulbach contributed to this report.

title: Ryan Garcia heads into Conor Benn fight as boxing's most divisive star | Opinion
description: Ryan Garcia embraces his status as boxing's most polarizing star and will put his WBC welterweight title on the line against Conor Benn Sept. 12.
fullText:
Ryan Garcia divides the world of boxing.

Love him or hate him, you're going to watch him.

Laud him or bash him, you care. (Maybe care more than you'll admit.)

He'll make you laugh, or make you scream. Regardless, Garcia will emerge from his welterweight title fight against Conor Benn Saturday, Sept. 12 with his reputation intact.

He is boxing's most polarizing star.

Garcia has offended Blacks, Jews, Muslims and the LGBTQ community with slurs. He has also entertained a cross-section of fans with his antics outside the ring and his powerful left hook inside it.

At 28, he has also split the Mexican community. He proudly embraces being Mexican-American even though he speaks limited Spanish. But everyone might agree that some of his behavior has been a little loco.

While many boxers show off their physiques during or after training sessions, Garcia poses in bath towels.

He's a pretty boy. A nasty puncher. A champion. And a chump.

As expected, Garcia has found new ways to fuel the polarization during the lead-up to his fight with Benn.

Nina Drama, the popular UFC personality, rendezvoused with Ryan Drama, er, Ryan Garcia and the hijinks ensued.

They danced. They danced some more. Garcia looked unconcerned about his fight while he munched on a huge burger.

"I know you can't do this Conor Benn,'' Garcia said, pointing at the burger. "You can't eat like I could eat.''

Benn, who as recently as November 2025 fought as a 160-pound middleweight, must weigh 147 pounds before the welterweight fight with Garcia. Garcia, who started his pro career in the 130-pound super featherweight division, will have no trouble making the weight, even after consuming a burger or two.

The moment was amusing. Or irritating. As is often the case, Garcia seemed to be no less committed to selling the right as preparing for the fight.

Nina Drama posted on X a video of Garcia's outside-the-ring hijinks and footage of Benn's intense training session.

"The difference between Ryan Garcia and Conor Benn training camps is actually hilarious LOL,'' Nina Drama wrote.

In July 2024, Garcia was expelled by the World Boxing Commission, one of the four boxing sanctioning bodies.

"We reject any form of discrimination,'' WBC president Mauricio Sulaimán said at the time in a statement.

On a Twitter Spaces that week, Garcia directed slurs at the Black and Muslim communities. He also made disparaging remarks about George Floyd, a Black man who died in 2020 after a Minneapolis police officer, who is White, knelt on his neck for more than nine minutes.

During that same month, Garcia made disparaging remarks about gay people and incendiary remarks about transgender people.

In November, the WBC lifted its ban on Garcia.

A statement issued on Sulaimán's X account read, "The WBC has been very close to Ryan, his family, management and promoter and we trust a new life inside and outside the ring will begin.''

Garcia demolished Devin Haney, knocking him down three times during a convincing victory in 2024. But then Garcia tested positive for a banned substance, overturning his victory and getting banned from boxing for a year.

In February, Garcia soundly defeated Mario Barrios and won the WBC world welterweight title – the first championship belt of Garcia's pro career. But the haters still will point to Garcia's fight against Gervonta "Tank" Davis in 2023. Davis drilled Garcia with a body shot that dropped Garcia to one knee.

Garcia appeared to make no effort to get back on his feet. A quitter, howled Garcia's critics.

But the so-called quitter is 25-2 with 20 knockouts and a championship belt.

Of course, it's not all about boxing that defines Garcia. It's the delusional and deranged rants on social media that led up to his fight with Haney. It's the arrest for vandalism at the Waldorf Astoria Beverly Hills hotel.

It was a surprise appearance in the wrestling ring during an episode of Monday Night RAW, which raises a question.

Is Ryan Garcia the heel worthy of boos? Or the champ worthy of cheers?

The inability to settle that debate is what helps elevate Garcia onto a polarizing perch.

title: The hugs at Shea Stadium that still define former Met’s post-9/11 memories
description: Hugs at midfield amidst the chaos and the moment Todd Zeile realized his own kids needed to have this story from him and not a just history book.
fullText:
Thinking back about that moment in time, Todd Zeile doesn't talk about the at-bats, the Mike Piazza home run or even the nervousness from that Sept. 21, 2001 game. The first Major League Baseball contest played in New York City after the Sept. 11 terror attacks has been boiled down to those video clips over the years.

But, Zeile, who started at first base that night for the New York Mets, remembers the hugs.

The Mets' first game back at Shea after the attacks was a huge moment for a city that had not had any normalcy in the 10 days since two airliners hit the World Trade Center and sent them crumbling to the ground. Piazza's home run that gave the Mets a 3-2 win that night became the signature image for the nation and history, but for the players on the field it was the emotions.

For Zeile, it was an impromptu moment long before then. Nobody planned it, but after the moment of silence and the national anthem, the players all walked to the middle of the field. The Braves and Mets players met and hugged before the game began.

"It was completely improved, organic hugs in the middle of the field, with guys that were our arch nemesis. It became less about the competition of that game and more about sportsmanship and camaraderie of guys from all over seeing the same thing. The beauty of the moment," Zeile said.

That moment, or really the emotions of all the moments, days, weeks, months and even years after the shock of the attacks is what has Zeile looking back now 25 years later as an executive producer on MLB Network's "When America Took the Field," debuting Thursday, Sept. 10 at 10 p.m. ET.

Zeile took about a decade off after retiring in 2004 to build his production company. He spent two seasons as co-executive producer on FX's "Anger Management" with Charlie Sheen. He got back into baseball as a guest analyst for SNY's Mets coverage.

Now was the time for him to combine both his baseball and film experience to make sure those moments are preserved as well as the Piazza home run and George W. Bush first pitch at the 2001 World Series.

"This, not just the documentary, just us being alive and going through this period, is the closest thing to the history being made in real time," he said. "people are going to read about it and know about it, and I am like 'Oh yeah, I was there for that. I saw that. I felt that.'"

That's why every anniversary he and his Mets teammates, who were at Ground Zero and New York City firehouses in the days after, keep telling their stories. So people don't forget.

Zeile wants to make sure his children and the next generations learn about what happened in the aftermath and the small part baseball played in the recovery.

That brought him back to New York, so he returned to the firehouses he visited in the aftermath of the attacks. He met the young firefighters who were the kids of the firefighters who were at Ground Zero. He saw their pride of carrying on that tradition and keeping the memories alive. That sparked his motivation about getting this on film while those who lived through it are still here to tell the stories for these kids.

Andrew Brenner directed the documentary and he had to figure out how to tell the story of one of the most infamous events in recent history with a fresh lens.

What Zeile and Brennen wanted from the film wasn't another retelling of the 10 days everybody knows about: Shea Stadium as a staging area for rescue workers and the Piazza home run. The pieces he was interested in were the ones that "had been at least lost or never told."

He wanted to make sure the story was about the months and years after, the "continued involvement and the continued passion that baseball as a whole has had for the (9/11) community." That's the community he lived through it with in 2001 and the families that are still connected to it now. That thread is what made the collaboration with MLB feel so different to him.

Zeile admits he was not sure baseball should have been played so soon after the attacks. Nobody was. What changed his mind is the trip the players took to Ground Zero.

"I recognized that the fire department and police department needed a little bit of a break from what they were doing, and baseball gave them that reprieve," he said. "It gave up more confidence to not feel like we were intruding or doing something that could be deemed inappropriate."

And after, as the Mets hit the road, something unusual happened.

"There certainly was a sense of pride, because we were representing New York and wherever we went guys (from other teams) would ask us 'What's it like there?' Or say 'I like that you are wearing the (NYPD and FDNY) hats' or 'How's the city?'" Zeile said. "It gave us an identity that was a little bit different, maybe a responsibility, in our interactions with other teams."

Those moments and the community that came out of the tragedy is what Zeile hopes people remember from this film.

They found three families with connections to baseball that were affected by the tragedy, they told the story of Joe Maddon, who was on the West Coast, but who lost a dear friend on one of the planes, and they found the story of the Secret Service agent who dressed up as an umpire and went on the field for George W. Bush's emotional first pitch of Game 3 of the 2001 World Series at Yankee Stadium.

Brenner, who was 22 and in Hoboken on that day, remembers driving out of town and listening to the news on the radio. He said that he and Zeile used those memories and emotions, but also wanted to zoom out from just those moments in New York that have been so well documented.

One moment from making the film that has stayed with Brennen more than any other was of a boy who was nine at the time of the attacks. He is one of the families woven through the documentary and he told the film crew that he can no longer separate what he actually remembers about that day from what he's simply been told happened.

"When he said that, it really struck me that putting together a film like this gives people like that a chance to learn," Brennen said. "It's so personal, so raw, they share these gut-wrenching emotions with us. But at certain times, they don't really know exactly what happened.

"It's a great way for people to learn some new stories and never forget."

title: Parkinson demands more from Wrexham after draw
description: Manager Phil Parkinson acknowledges Wrexham have room for improvement after they were held to a 1-1 draw at home by Burnley.
fullText:
Manager Phil Parkinson acknowledged Wrexham have room for improvement after they were held to a 1-1 draw at home by Burnley.

Jacques Ekomie's second-half header saw the Red Dragons come from behind to earn a point against a side who started the evening bottom of the Championship.

Wrexham are unbeaten in three games but are still searching for their first win of the season at the Racecourse.

"There are things we can do better," said Parkinson, whose side went into the fixture after a 3-0 win at Millwall and 0-0 draw at Swansea.

"Without the ball, tactically we didn't get it quite right. They changed a couple of things and we were also a bit passive in terms of the way we pressed as well.

"It was a combination of those two factors and if you look at the Swansea and Millwall games we restricted two teams to hardly a shot on goal.

"Against Burnley there was just a bit too much space in areas and we need to look at that.

"We got caught 10 to 15 yards too deep at times. At half-time we rectified that and the pressing was loads better."

Wrexham are away to another side relegated from the Premier League, leaders West Ham United, on Friday evening (20:00 BST).

There are doubts over the availability of Max Cleworth and Josh Windass after injuries against Burnley, but Parkinson is hopeful the blows are not too serious.

Defender Cleworth came off after half an hour while forward Windass did not come back out for for the second half.

"Max looks like his hamstring's tightened up and Josh got a kick on the calf," Parkinson added.

"[Max] he felt it early in the half actually and we kept saying to him 'are you alright' and he wanted to stay on. I don't think it's too serious, but we'll see.

"Josh had got a whack on the calf and when you've made one sub in the first period, you've only got then two entries in the second period.

"He probably could have gone out and tried it, but we just decided to make the change then."

title: White confirms MVP exit after UFC contract expires
description: British fighter Michael 'Venom' Page is leaving the UFC after seeing out his contract, its president Dana White confirms.
fullText:
British fighter Michael 'Venom' Page is leaving the UFC, its president Dana White has confirmed.

The 39-year-old, who is nicknamed MVP, joined MMA's top promotion in December 2023 on a six-fight contract.

He concluded that deal with an underwhelming win over Nursulton Ruziboev on Saturday amid booing from the crowd in Paris.

Page has a 5-1 record with UFC, fighting at welterweight and middleweight, but all five of those wins have come via decision and he has admitted to not delivering "what I wanted to deliver".

Although the Londoner was keen to discuss his future with the UFC, he was removed from their rankings after Saturday's fight.

White has now added: "That was his last fight on his contract. I don't think we're signing him, no.

"What's the confusion? I think it's been pretty clear that he wasn't being re-signed and that he would be taken out of the rankings because he's no longer on the roster."

With the former Bellator fighter now a free agent, he could join the PFL or turn to boxing.

White has also said the UFC will not wait for heavyweight champion Tom Aspinall to return to action.

The British fighter is still recovering from eye injuries sustained in his fight against Cyril Gane almost a year ago.

The 33-year-old's return date is unknown but he has been cleared to return to training and says he has no plans to leave the UFC or retire.

"I mean, Tom Aspinall is hurt until we hear differently so the heavyweight division will just keep rolling," said White.

Gane claimed the interim heavyweight title with a second-round stoppage of Alex Pereira in June and the Brazilian has said he wants a rematch with the 36-year-old Frenchman.

If Aspinall remains out for the rest of 2026, White hinted Gane could take another bout in his absence.

title: Where Estevao fits into Chelsea's all-star attack
description: A look at where Estevao Willian could feature for Chelsea this season after the reminder of his quality in his cameo against Arsenal.
fullText:
A late flourish from Estevao Willian almost snatched Chelsea a draw at Arsenal on Sunday.

His curling strike was saved by goalkeeper David Raya to preserve Arsenal's lead, but it served as a reminder of the important role the 19-year-old Brazil winger could play in Xabi Alonso's side.

His game time has been limited so far this season by the club record £117m signing of Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa as well as the form of Cole Palmer and Joao Pedro.

The £51m signing from Brazilian club Palmeiras has played only 96 minutes this season, with 80 of those coming against League One side Luton Town in the Carabao Cup.

His remaining 16 minutes were in substitute appearances against Fulham and Premier League champions Arsenal, while he was unused as Chelsea held on for a narrow victory over Brighton in their third match of the campaign.

Reports in Brazil have suggested Estevao is unhappy with his lack of opportunities.

However, those claims have been denied by sources at Stamford Bridge and by people close to the player, some of whom have also expressed excitement about Chelsea's summer recruitment - including the arrival of Rogers.

Chelsea regard Estevao as one of a small group of untouchable players that includes Palmer, Joao Pedro and Moises Caicedo.

The club have no intention of selling any of them, with Estevao central to the long-term planning of Alonso and Chelsea's leadership team.

There were also early discussions over a new contract, with Chelsea keen to reward key players with improved terms in the coming months, having done so for Joao Pedro.

Asked whether Estevao's lack of involvement meant he was unhappy, Alonso replied: "No, Este is ready, training well. The other day he had a great impact.

"He is fully involved with a very good attitude every day. I count on Este 100% because of his potential. He is so young but he is learning and adapting quickly. The season is long."

Estevao also suffered a serious grade-four hamstring tear late last season and missed the World Cup, so is expected to build his involvement through the campaign.

Chelsea explored move for Fulham midfielder Berge

Two right-backs in midfield - are Chelsea short despite £349m spent?

Estevao came on for Pedro Neto, who has been operating as a wing-back in Alonso's new system, as Chelsea chased an equaliser on Sunday.

It is difficult to imagine any other in-game circumstance in which Estevao would be asked to perform the same role, given the defensive and physical demands placed on players in that position.

Instead, Palmer occupies Estevao's preferred inside-right number 10 role.

Estevao and Palmer have shown encouraging signs when used together when Alonso has played a back four - but he has deployed that shape only against Luton Town in the Carabao Cup.

Displacing Palmer for league games could prove difficult as Alonso regards him as both a dressing-room leader and one of his key attacking threats.

Alonso has also fielded close to his strongest side even in the Carabao Cup, with Chelsea not involved in European competition and with the new head coach eager to establish his tactical principles as quickly as possible following his arrival.

Estevao is not alone in struggling for meaningful minutes early in the season and, should Leeds United win at Stamford Bridge in the Carabao Cup on Wednesday, the Blues will have no further cup fixtures until the FA Cup in January.

That quietly makes Wednesday's game an important one in terms of keeping a 27-man squad satisfied.

Some of Chelsea's other young attackers have also struggled to start matches, with Palmer and Rogers beginning every game.

Joao Pedro has started all three league matches, while experienced striker Danny Welbeck led the line against Luton. That has limited Emmanuel Emegha, who joined from Strasbourg in the summer, to only one appearance on the bench.

Similarly, defender Aaron Anselmino is also yet to play and was only included in one squad, albeit both players are managing fitness issues.

Other attacking options, including Geovany Quenda and Jamie Gittens, have featured for only eight and 10 minutes respectively across Chelsea's four matches this season.

Quenda, who was signed despite interest from Manchester United in 2024, has also been left out of two of Alonso's matchday squads.

The situation might be even more challenging if it not for fitness issues affecting Moises Caicedo and Jordan Henderson, which have at times left Chelsea short in midfield.

Even then, summer signing Valentin Barco has been restricted to one start and a substitute appearance, as right-back Malo Gusto has started in midfield instead. Wing-back Marco Palestra also remains out injured.

If Chelsea had a fully fit squad available, they would have to leave six outfield players out of their matchday squad, with clubs permitted to name 11 starters and nine substitutes in English football.

Analysis of successful teams playing without European football suggests managers often rely on a relatively small core group of players.

Leicester City's surprise Premier League title-winning side of 2015-16 was achieved with only 14 players making more than 15 appearances in all competitions under Claudio Ranieri.

The following season, Chelsea won the title under Antonio Conte without European commitments. Only 13 players accumulated more than 1,500 minutes in all competitions.

While clubs are now allowed to make five substitutions, only 14 Newcastle United players exceeded the 1,500-minute mark when they qualified for the Champions League in 2022-23.

Perhaps the most relevant comparison is Manchester United after they finished third last season without European football. Only 13 players recorded more than 1,500 minutes across all competitions, although they exited both domestic cup competitions at an early stage.

For those on the fringes, including Estevao, a prolonged cup run could aide their chances of turning brief cameos into opportunities that Alonso cannot ignore.

title: Osaka makes passionate defence of on-court outfits

Naomi Osaka says any criticism she receives for her extravagant outfits is "worth it" if it means "the people after me have an easier path".

In her latest outfit, Japan's four-time Grand Slam champion wore a decorated coat at the start of her last-16 US Open defeat by Elena Rybakina.

In defending her fashion statements, she referred to speaking out about her mental health in 2021 when she refused to speak to the media at the French Open and subsequently withdrew from the tournament.

Osaka, whose father is Haitian-American and mother is Japanese, also highlighted her ancestry.

"I don't mind being the first to do something and getting trashed for it," she wrote in a social media post.

"This happened when I talked about mental health and for some reason it's happening with my clothes lol.

title: Rangers eye second place as Celtic set pace
description: Rangers host St Mirren, while Celtic travel to Perth to take on St Johnstone in Wednesday's Premiership action.
fullText:
With the Old Firm in action on Wednesday, the Scottish Premiership table will have a familiar look if Rangers can make it four successive wins.

The Ibrox outfit host St Mirren, while Celtic travel to Perth to take on St Johnstone.

Derek McInnes' side appear to be finding their feet after dropping points in their opening two league outings and falling out of Europe.

Meanwhile, Celtic have a perfect domestic record, bouncing back from a Champions League qualifying trauma in Austria and adding an array of new faces at the end of the transfer window.

The Glasgow rivals meet at Ibrox on Sunday in the quarter-finals of the Premier Sports Cup, so how will they warm up for the first derby of the season?

Rangers find themselves trailing third-placed St Mirren on goal difference, following a bright start from the Paisley side.

Head coach Craig McLeish has earned plaudits for implementing a more fluid style and he was named Premiership manager of the month for August.

"I'm not surprised it's come together so quickly - I get that from the outside it might look like that," McLeish said.

"There's an internal belief about what we're doing and the work we can do on the pitch. It could have been even better and we were close to it being even better."

However, the Buddies have already been to Ibrox this season and were soundly thrashed in the Premier Sports Cup.

James Penrice enjoyed a lively Rangers debut that day, scoring one of five goals and setting up another.

The left-back has started each game since, along with central defenders Olwethu Makhanya and Emmanuel Fernandez. While the latter is prone to the odd wobble, a settled defence has provided a platform for the recent upturn in results.

Motherwell rarely threatened at Ibrox on Saturday as Rangers spurned several good opportunities to increase their lead.

That result came after wins over Aberdeen and Falkirk. McInnes says confidence is building while admitting there is still a pressure to succeed.

"I don't think that ever lifts until you've got a trophy in your hand," he said.

"But I do think there's been a good feel about the place. What we have had in recent weeks is just small steps, encouragement, confidence levels."

The loss of Lawrence Shankland to injury just as the striker had found his shooting boots is a blow, so Kevin Kelsy may not have the luxury of easing himself into his new surroundings.

Rangers won the previous two league games against St Mirren by the odd goal but prior to that the visitors had an unbeaten streak of four in this fixture.

Celtic had to work hard for their weekend win in Paisley, with McLeish's team impressive between both boxes but lacking a killer touch.

St Mirren will be without the bite of Paul Nsio, who can't play against his parent club, and that could be telling since Rangers had the run of midfield in that cup tie last month.
