Rangers lose Shankland for up to four months

How much will Celtic miss Asian Games-bound Yang?

Celtic were far from their flowing best on Saturday evening but got the job done after falling behind.

Yang Hyun-jun was the star man, capping an energetic display with the decisive finish, but the winger is now away with South Korea for the Asian Games.

His absence will mean a reshuffle but Martin O'Neill may be reluctant to shift Camilo Duran out wide again after a run of three goals and two assists in three games at centre-forward. If he does, on-loan Chelsea striker Shim Mheuka could make his first start.

Of the six players arriving in the final 48 hours of the window only Mheuka and Oliver Sorensen have been used from the bench so far and it could be that Sebastian Tounekti is the safe choice to replace Yang.

Striker Kasper Hogh and left-back Kieran Tierney are also in contention after brief spells out injured.

The champions can expect to face another side who focus on possession and playing through the phases as St Johnstone hunt a third win on the bounce at McDiarmid Park.

"They want to play football as well and they're committed," O'Neill said of Celtic's next opponents.

"There's a vitality about them which is very encouraging. Not dissimilar in many aspects to what Craig McLeish is doing at St Mirren."

Three of Josh Fowler's four goals have come in Perth, while local lad Taylor Steven caught the eye with his crossing from the right in victory over Hibs.

Centre-backs Cheick Diabate and Zach Mitchell are a no-nonsense pair who will put their heads where it hurts, although Saints are yet to keep a league clean sheet.

Head coach Simo Valakari admits they will need a degree of fortune to continue their impressive home form.

"We need to do our football things so well, then at the same time, we need to earn our luck, because against Celtic, if you want to beat them, you need to be a little bit lucky in some moments," the Finn said.

O'Neill was last in Perth as a manager 25 years ago but you don't have to go back very far for the most recent upset, given a home win over Celtic in April 2025 was among the rare moments of joy in a season that ended in relegation for St Johnstone.

title: 'Bottling it' - Garcia no-show for first Benn face-off
description: Conor Benn said Ryan Garcia "bottled" their first face-off after the American failed to turn up to their meeting on Tuesday in Las Vegas.
fullText:
Ryan Garcia was a no-show for his first face-off with Conor Benn on Tuesday before their world title fight this weekend in Las Vegas.

The American was scheduled to attend a photo opportunity, but skipped it to leave Benn appearing alone.

Benn, 29, did have the company of his father, boxing legend Nigel Benn, who pretended to face off with his son.

After joking around with his dad, Benn said Garcia "didn't turn up".

"I apologise for Ryan doing what Ryan does and bottling it. We turn up, we're here, ready for the face-off," he said.

"Come Saturday, he's in for a war."

Garcia defends his WBC welterweight title at the T-Mobile Arena in Benn's first world championship bout.

The 28-year-old is the favourite for the contest and after failing to attend the first face-off of fight week, Garcia mocked Benn on Instagram.

"Nice relaxing time as Conor wastes time showing up to a face-off," he said.

"Back to the sauna you go, sausage getting cooked every way."

They are due to meet twice before fight night with the news conference on Thursday and the weigh-in on Friday.

Much has been made of Benn's weight cut for this contest, with the Briton having not fought at 10st 7lb (67kg) since 2022.

Benn had two fights with Chris Eubank Jr at middleweight before a 10st 12lb (69kg) catchweight against Regis Prograis in April.

Garcia has fought at lightweight and light-welterweight – missing weight for his light-welterweight contest against Devin Haney in 2024 – but is not expected to have issues with the weight, while Benn has said he does not intend to stay long at welterweight.

In the co-main event on Saturday, Jai Opetaia is fighting Noel Mikaelian in a cruiserweight bout.

Mikaelian is the WBC champion, but could be stripped of the belt after withdrawing from his bout against the mandatory challenger in favour of facing the Australian.

Saturday's fight is further complicated by promoter Don King, who claims he has an exclusive deal with Mikaelian.

The veteran American promoter has sent a cease-and-desist letter to Zuffa Boxing and demanded the fight be cancelled.

Confirming Zuffa Boxing had received the legal letter, Dana White insisted the bout would be going ahead as planned.

title: McLaren talks, 'numb' cars and being 'captain of the ship' - Verstappen Q&A
description: In an exclusive interview with BBC Sport, Max Verstappen talks about his new contract at Red Bull and much more.
fullText:
Max Verstappen is in a no-nonsense mood - even more than usual.

The Red Bull driver is renowned for his straight talking but now, as he discusses his 2026 season so far in an exclusive interview with BBC Sport, he is at his most uncompromising.

We're talking on the eve of last weekend's Italian Grand Prix. The temperature is into the mid-30Cs, Red Bull's hospitality unit is not coping well, and Verstappen's PR handler messages before the Dutchman turns up to suggest I find a table near a fan; the interview might be more positive that way.

Monza is the second race since the four-time world champion signed a two-year contract extension with Red Bull.

In theory, this runs to the end of 2030. In reality, it changes little. It still has performance clauses. So Verstappen is earning a bit more money but, if Red Bull are still struggling for competitiveness next year, there will remain the prospect he could look for pastures new.

Verstappen arrives and briefly adjusts the fan blowing in our direction. "It's too hot in here," he says.

Does he need a breather before we start? "No, no," he says. "I'm good. It was just that it was super-hot in the corner when I was doing the print [media]."

Verstappen is always a great interviewee. Direct, honest, uncompromising.

Now, for whatever reason, he is especially frank and open, as we discuss why he extended his contract, his discussions with McLaren, his stunning appearance at the Nurburgring 24 Hours in May, and the new Formula 1 engine rules, with which it is no secret he has a problem.

Where's your head at, Max, in terms of how the season has gone so far?

"Of course it's not where I want to be, but as a team we're trying to just learn and understand a lot of things for next year. We are not in a title fight. We are just trying to find more performance.

"Changes need to happen to the car for next year. We will not be able to change that for this year, but we just need to try and get a lot of learnings to do better next year."

"Overall we're just lacking a bit of performance. The car is not where I want it to be feeling-wise, and the through-corner balance is too hit and miss between entry, mid and exit.

"It's just fundamentally something in the car that we need to try and work on for the next year."

This has been a bit of a theme for longer than this year. How concerning is it that that's happening across a different set of regulations?

"That's exactly that. There's also things that we talk about within the team, like how can that happen, how can we fix it? That's basically what we are doing now and trying to do now.

"Some people have left, new people have come in. With the new people, we are discussing what we can do about it. Is that just some changes, a different philosophy? All these kind of things."

What made you sign a new contract?

"It comes down to also feeling well within a team. This is like a second family to me.

"The belief that you can turn things around, you can build towards hopefully a better future with other people, new people. And at the end of the day, it's not only Formula 1 for me. There are a lot of things that I'm doing next year that Red Bull is involved in as well.

"I feel good here. So this, for me, is the right place to be."

Did it take much for them to convince you to do it?

"I always said to them: 'Don't stress about it, just work on the car.' Because the faster the car goes, the easier the decision is anyway.

"I can understand, of course, maybe sometimes they were a little bit worried. But at the same time, for me, I was just worried about here, what was going on.

"At the same time, I was very busy with my stuff also outside of Formula 1. So I never really spent a lot of time talking or doing different things or trying to go somewhere else."

From the outside, it's hard to see what they could have done to convince you things will improve.

"I don't mind the challenge also. I don't have that desire or need to show in another car that I can win it, or whatever.

"It's easy to run to the fastest car and then do it all again. But it's not how I am. You cannot be the captain of the ship and as soon as there is something not working, you jump off the ship.

"It's been a bit downwards from the dominant years, but I don't mind also rebuilding it. It's another challenge as well."

You talked to Mercedes last year, McLaren this year. How serious was that?

"Of course, any kind of chat you take seriously. They're all very respectful chats. There's nothing wrong with that.

"I felt that staying was, for me, the right choice. You have to follow your heart. I could have run away very early on in my Red Bull career and gone somewhere else to try and win. If you have a little bit of patience, you do end up winning. I feel like that's my approach now as well."

What race have you enjoyed most this year?

"Probably the Nordschleife [Nurburgring 24 Hours]. It was super-cool to be able to do an endurance event with my team-mates, the guys that won with the car throughout the main season.

"We knew that we were going to be really strong. We peaked at the right time, but unfortunately the car retired. It was an incredible experience. And pure. Pure motorsport."

Your first stint, where you went from 10th to first, was so impressive.

"I was enjoying it. Not easy conditions. It started to drizzle. The track was slippery. Crashes. Code 60s [when a stretch of track is limited to 60km/h after an incident].

"Some people were like: 'Let's see how he will do in the race under pressure with all these kinds of scenarios that he has never done before.'

"But I have done them a million times on the simulator. I have done so many laps and 24-hour races on the simulator. I never felt out of depth or whatever. I was fully zoned in. I just had a great time.

"Once I was in the race, you switch to another level. I was just in a zone. It's really enjoyable."

You want to go back to Nurburgring to win that race. Is there anything else on your bucket list?

"All the endurance races. Eventually, of course also Hypercar [the world endurance championship]. I don't want to rush it. I want to do it in the right environment. On my terms. And competitive."

Is it true you want to do Le Mans with Fernando Alonso?

"We've talked about it. I mean, look at Fernando. He's 45 and he's still flying. Especially for Le Mans, with his experience, it could be a good option. It needs to fit our schedules. It needs to make sense. It needs to be on my terms. And there needs to be a real chance to go there and win it."

You have been clear about your distaste for the new F1 engine rules this year and at the Japanese Grand Prix you said: 'Is it worth it?' What convinced you it was?

"Hoping that it will be better in the future. Accepting where we are at the moment. Still the love for the sport. Not at the moment the driving. But the love for the sport.

"I love competition, naturally. I just hope that in the coming years, towards 2030, it can only get better. And to start to make the best of it, because these are the rules for the next four or five years."

So that people can understand why the drivers have been upset this year, what is it about these hybrid engines, and the need to recharge the batteries, that detracts from the best drivers' abilities?

"In the history of the sport, normally the driver that is the most committed, the latest on the brakes, earlier on throttle, committing in the high speed, they get rewarded, because you just gain that time in the corner.

"But now you're constantly thinking about, 'In this corner I might have to hold in a bit. Go later on throttle. Or brake earlier. Or lift off. And then I have more top speed.' Stuff like that. It's so unnatural. It's so not how it should be.

"No disrespect. And I hope no-one picks up on this. But look at Yuki [Tsunoda]. He jumps in the [Racing Bulls] car [at the Dutch Grand Prix]. Never driven the car before. Immediately competitive.

"Liam [Lawson] jumps from the Racing Bulls to the Red Bull - immediately competitive. It's because these cars are numb to your driver inputs.

"Of course, yes, you still have to do a good lap. And you still have to commit. The fastest drivers will always come out on top. But it's really, really limited, like a choke hold or something. You're held back."

Formula 1 as a sport has accepted that it needs to change, and the internal combustion-electrical split is changing to 60-40 in two steps by 2028. But what would you like to see for the new engine formula 1 in 2030 or 2031?

"It has to go back to a V8, just for drivability already. When you drive the old cars, you cannot imagine the difference in how the engine responds, or the drivability you get. And how terrible or horrible it actually is now compared to just having a V8."

What about compared to last year's turbo-hybrid engines?

"Also horrible, the feeling compared to a V8. The V8 is so much better. It is so much more free, lighter. Cars are so heavy nowadays.

"It is better to just have a smaller V8 engine, much lighter. Try to really limit the battery size to maybe like a kind of push-to-pass battery. But you should not have it involved or any kind of proper normal performance running."

And you would have no turbo either?

"Ideally not, because that introduces turbo lag."

So what do you enjoy about F1 these days? The competition and prestige more than the actual purity of the racing?

"I have been lucky that the years before have been quite decent [in terms of results]. Not how I wanted it to be with the battery side of things.

"But just the emotion of the V8, of the V10, back in the day, when I was a kid. You walk around, you hear these cars go out, you have goosebumps.

"Even if you go 300km/h compared to now sometimes 350, 360, it doesn't matter.

"It is the emotion of the noise that you get from these cars, of the vibration. It is just another level. And I really hope that that thing will come back."

People see you as a kind of winning machine. But obviously your character is much more complex than that. Can you explain that contradiction?

"I am a winning machine when I need to be. But I can also switch off, and enjoy my life outside of racing.

"But anything racing-related, of course I am a winning machine. I demand a lot from the people in the team. They also expect me to perform and do the best job I can.

"That is what you get paid for at the end of the day. We have the same target. The same goal.

"Of course I can be very outspoken. But that is what I like. That is also with our culture.

"And that is how I approach my life also outside of F1, with my GT3 team. We do not hold back. At least for me, you need to be like that to really get the best out of everyone."

Why is speaking your mind and being honest so important to you?

"I just want to be myself. I know there are a lot of politics in Formula 1, and I understand also between the teams there are a lot of politics.

"You will always speak for yourself in terms of where you think you might have an advantage or not as a team. That is normal. Also with the engines and the chassis, it is the same thing.

"When it is good, it is good. When it is bad, it is bad. You will hear it from me because that is how I like to operate. And I am not holding back from that."

title: Are women better than men at endurance running?
description: Women have beaten men in some high-profile endurance events in recent months - are they better suited to these challenges?
fullText:
"The race is too hard for women. They are simply not tough enough to do it."

Those are the words of Lazarus Lake, race director of the Barkley Marathons - one of the world's hardest ultramarathons which to date, of the approximate 1,000 people who have started, only 20 have ever completed.

Speaking in 2015 and daring for someone to prove him wrong, it took nine years until a British ultra-runner did just that.

Completing the extreme 100-mile course with just one minute 39 seconds to spare of the 60-hour cut-off, Jasmin Paris from Midlothian made history and cemented her name in the ultra-running history books.

But now, increasingly, she is not alone.

Last summer, there was a female one-two for the first time in the gruelling Montane Summer Spine Race from Derbyshire to Scotland. Rachel Entrekin set a new course record and became the first woman to win the Cocodona 250 in Arizona in May, while last month Sophie Woods smashed the overall record by six days to complete the Via Alpina.

It appears female runners are no longer just taking part in ultra-endurance events, they are competing with their male counterparts, breaking records and in some cases, winning races outright.

All of this has prompted suggestions that they are perhaps better suited to these kinds of challenges.

But is there any scientific proof? Do women really have any physiological or psychological advantages in endurance exercise (anything that takes more than six hours)? And if so, could we see more of these records fall in the future?

In running distances up to the marathon, there is on average a 10-12% performance gap between males and females.

Men are generally stronger and built with a bigger aerobic engine.

But as the distance increases, those physical advantages appear to become less relevant and the gap starts to narrow.

The "gender pace gap" diminishes to 0.25% in 100-mile races, according to a study of more than 20 years of amateur ultra-race data conducted by RunRepeat, in collaboration with the International Association of Ultrarunners,

Anything further than 195 miles and women have the potential to be faster.

For Professor Andy Jones, an expert in endurance performance at the University of Exeter, there are three potential physiological explanations why women could perform better over longer distances or durations.

Fat metabolism – women have higher fat stores and burn it more efficiently, giving them a steady energy source for longer.

Muscles – women have more oxygen-efficient muscle fibres, known as "slow twitch", that are better suited for endurance activities.

Fatigue resistance – women retain more strength over hours of endurance exercise.

However, Jones, who played a key role in Eliud Kipchoge's sub two-hour marathon challenge in 2019, is keen to point out that the science in this area is "behind".

"There isn't as much hard evidence as there would be for shorter distances, which have been studied for a long time in quite some detail," he adds.

That is a view shared by Dr Richard Burden, co-lead of female athlete health and performance at the UK Sports Institute, who feels a lot more information needs to be gathered before conclusions can be made.

"At the moment we are speculating … there are definitely some physiological adaptations that you see 

Physiology, however, only gets you so far. The realities of ultra-endurance exercise - multi-day events, sleep deprivation, extreme terrain and conditions, to name but a few – mean the journey to the finish line is as much mental as it is physical.

And for Sophie Woods, this is where women have the edge.

"It's not necessarily about being the fastest person at the start," she says. "It is about preparation, it is about mental strength and being able to continue to persevere when things go wrong."

During the New Zealand runner's record-breaking run of the Via Alpina, she was forced to expect the unexpected – from disruption caused by wildfires that made her route longer and more dangerous to swarms of horseflies.

"I was so tired and there were so many of them and I wanted to have a complete meltdown and just cry, but I couldn't because if I stopped moving, they started biting me," she says.

"I think women are really good at adapting and continuing and just knowing that once we start something, you've just got to keep moving until you get to the finish."

That view is echoed by Yngvild Kaspersen, who last month became the first woman to win the prestigious Ultra-Trail Mont Blanc CCC race in the Alps twice. She credits her victory to the "mental game" she puts herself through in training.

The Norwegian, who balances life as a professional runner with her job as a GP, also believes female ultra-runners are so strong because camaraderie in the community is unrivalled.

"We're competitors but we're also motivating each other, inspiring each other, pushing each other to do better in the races," she says. "If you see the podiums for the women this year [at UTMB], how close we are and how we're running together out there - that's very special and I'm very proud to be a part of that community and that group of women."

So can we explain why women might be more resilient?

Sports dietitian Renee McGregor, who specialises in athlete nutrition and hormonal health, believes the answer comes from the female body itself.

"The moment women step into puberty, we are dealing with a fluctuating hormonal system," she says. "We never ever give ourselves credit for that, it's just an accepted part of being female. But actually, it is an endurance in itself and I think that's probably where a big part of our resilience comes from."

McGregor, an ultra-runner herself, points to research that suggests female runners display more disciplined and even pacing strategies than men in distance races, maximising on what she terms the female "brain bank".

"I don't think women go into these races without a lot of thought and contingency planning," McGregor adds.

"For example, if you've been through a pregnancy and you've dealt with nausea, if you've had a baby and dealt with the lack of sleep or if you've gone through fertility treatment, you have to go through so much discomfort, but you know you can get through it. And I think it's that knowledge of 'I can get through this, I can find a solution'."

One of the biggest reasons why we cannot talk with any certainty about the potential physiological and psychological advantages that women may have in this field is because participation numbers are low, with women making up roughly only 20% of those on ultramarathon start lines.

Research by SheRACES, a network set up by British ultra-runner Sophie Power to correct gender disparities in running, suggests the reasons for this range from societal perceptions around women's abilities, to concerns around the time needed for training, or access to the right support at the events themselves.

Slowly but surely, however, things are starting to change.

Earlier this year, a trail race in New Zealand became the first UTMB World Series event to achieve a 50:50 gender split, while a leading UK race provider has launched a new initiative to target gender parity at its events.

And now, according to Dr Burden, society is talking about the limits of human performance in a different way too.

"Historically, the majority of the time it [the limits of the human] will be established from male models or male sports," he says. "Now we're starting to break it up into the limits of male performance and the limits of female performance and that's a distinction that needs to be made … but to make better comparisons, we would need more women taking part in ultra events."

The runner who went viral and sparked a campaign for change for women

Mashed potato & 19 minutes' sleep - Entrekin's epic race

When it comes to participation, visibility is key.

Kaspersen describes Rachel Entrekin's historic victory at Cocodona 250, one of the most demanding ultramarathons in the world, as an "inspiration" among the elites to "dare to try".

And at the amateur level, there are those like Emily Fairs, a 22-year-old ultra-runner who documents the realities of her training and races on social media as part of her mission to get more women of all ages on start lines.

"When it comes to endurance training, there are so many components that come into it and that we are fearful of but by seeing another woman do it you think 'right, if she can do it, if she has the tools, she has the knowledge, she has the ability to do all these crazy difficult challenges, then so do I. I'm no different to her. She's no different to me'," says Fairs.

Fairs says she has received thousands of messages from women about how her content has encouraged them to lace up their trainers, and believes recent trends of female success in ultra-running are just the start.

"When the proportion is so low, we have no clue what women are capable of. We're starting to see more women get faster and enter the sport and push themselves and break records. So, who knows where we'll be 10-15 years later down the line?"

title: Shelton beats Alcaraz in latest-ever US Open finish to reach semis
description: Carlos Alcaraz's US Open title defence is over after a dramatic five-set quarter-final loss to Ben Shelton which ends at 03:34 local time.
fullText:
Carlos Alcaraz's US Open title defence came to an end in a dramatic five-set quarter-final loss to Ben Shelton that ended at 03:34 local time - the latest finish in the tournament's history.

A large crowd remained captivated deep into the night as a modern classic unfolded over an unpredictable four hours and 28 minutes on Arthur Ashe Stadium.

The match did not begin until about 11pm in New York, after the start of the night session was delayed by Tuesday's earlier matches.

At its conclusion, eighth seed Shelton basked in a standing ovation from a delirious audience after completing a 6-7 (5-7) 6-1 6-3 1-6 7-6 (10-7) victory that will live long in the memory of all those present.

"That was a war, an epic match, so physical," Shelton said.

"Carlos is one of the greatest champions in our sport already at 23 years old.

"It's ridiculous some of the stuff he comes up with sometimes - the most enjoyable match that I've had in my career, for sure."

This was the biggest - and certainly most significant - win of Shelton's career.

He had not beaten a top-three player in 17 attempts, and had lost each of his three previous matches against Spain's Alcaraz.

It also boosted home hopes of a first American men's singles champion in New York for 23 years.

Shelton was less than a year old when Andy Roddick won the US Open in 2003 - but an American finalist is guaranteed when he and Frances Tiafoe meet in Friday's semi-finals.

World number three Alcaraz was competing at his first tournament since a lengthy injury lay-off, but that is to take nothing away from Shelton, who produced a phenomenal performance.

Seven-time major winner Alcaraz had exceeded expectations on his return after more than four months out with a wrist injury, including sweeping past 20th seed Tommy Paul to reach the last eight.

But the 23-year-old's lack of match fitness appeared to finally catch up with him in a high-octane encounter filled with breathless exchanges and astounding displays of athleticism.

Even when it appeared Alcaraz had emptied the tank, the two-time winner not only forced a deciding set but would go the distance as the players engaged in a tense 10-point match tie-break that provided a fitting conclusion to the contest.

"It was close. So I'm just not going to be disappointed about not getting the win at the end," said Alcaraz.

"I'm just proud about myself, about how I fought. I leave the court with a smile, healthy, and this is what I needed."

While home hope Shelton had the vast support of the hardy crowd, Alcaraz has always felt at home at Flushing Meadows.

The Spaniard had won 28 of his 31 matches at the tournament - the highest win rate at the US Open in the sport's professional era at above 90% - and last year became the first man to reach the final without dropping a set since Roger Federer in 2015.

The Australian Open champion was also on an 18-match unbeaten streak at Grand Slam tournaments, having missed the French Open and Wimbledon with injury, and was seeking to reach his fourth New York semi-final in five years.

Regardless of his opponent's current levels, for Shelton this was a victory that could prove seismic in front of a home crowd who passionately backed him throughout.

"It is incredible, I always say that this is the greatest stadium in the world," the 23-year-old said.

"I'm just hoping my best friend and sister don't have to be at work at 6am. It would be huge from their employers to let them have the day off."

The American number one is through to his third major semi-final, having lost to two of the game's heavyweights in Jannik Sinner at last year's Australian Open and Novak Djokovic in New York three years ago. Both went on to be crowned champions.

After ousting Alcaraz, Shelton is now the second-highest ranked player remaining in the draw after world number two Alexander Zverev.

It remains to be seen how Shelton will recover for the semi-final against Tiafoe, who completed a remarkable comeback from two sets and a break down to beat compatriot Alex Michelsen.

"For me, it's always about the people in the crowd - whether it's my coaches and my team, all of my family and friends," Shelton said.

"The city of New York that showed up tonight until 3am, that's what kept me going."

Sabalenka fights back to keep US Open defence alive

Osaka makes passionate defence of on-court outfits

A closely contested first set offered a hint of the momentum swings that would define the match.

Alcaraz edged the opener on a tie-break - but only after surrendering his advantage after breaking for a seemingly decisive 6-5 lead.

Shelton, however, was ruthless as Alcaraz's level dropped sharply and embarked on a run of nine unanswered games to claim the second set and take charge of the third.

Refusing to fold, Alcaraz launched his fourth-set revival by saving two break points and then breaking when Shelton missed a backhand.

Alcaraz appeared to be sick into his towel during a changeover, such was his level of physical exertion, but would break Shelton a second time as he earned a fifth set as the time approached 02:30.

Both players failed to take break-point opportunities before a match-deciding breaker swung back and forth.

Shelton led 3-1 and Alcaraz regained control at 5-3.

But the Spaniard's uncharacteristically high number of unforced errors - the second seed made 53 overall - ultimately cost him, as Shelton captured five of the next six points before seeing out victory in style with an ace.

The first sign that all was not well with Alcaraz came at the end of the first set.

His forehand was off, and his serve erratic. Some of the rallies were stunning, but he was playing carelessly at times, and sometimes seemed disengaged as his concentration fluctuated.

All of which can be expected of someone who was playing just his fifth singles match since April and a first against a top-10 player.

But the opponent has to take advantage - and Shelton did so superbly.

Shelton has previously had a miserable record against the very best, losing all 17 of his previous matches against top-three players.

The flashy left-hander played plenty of shots and sent down one serve at 149mph, but was excellent on return and disciplined in defence.

title: England to extend head coach Borthwick's contract
description: England head coach Steve Borthwick will have his contract extended past the 2028 Six Nations in a bid to avoid uncertainty over his future before and during next year's Rugby World Cup.
fullText:
England head coach Steve Borthwick will have his contract extended past the 2028 Six Nations in a bid to avoid uncertainty over his future before and during next year's Rugby World Cup.

As it did with Red Roses boss John Mitchell before the 2025 World Cup, the Rugby Football Union has moved to ensure Borthwick and his staff have some clarity over their positions going into the global showpiece.

According to RFU performance director Conor O'Shea, extending Borthwick's deal into the middle of 2028 will allow time to decide who leads the team in the longer-term.

"You don't want them looking for a job going into [a World Cup]," O'Shea explained.

"Everyone knows it will be judged on the World Cup, but you can't have a group of coaches going in with that uncertainty, especially when you look at the timing.

"So we will give that certainty, and that will give us time to look properly."

In a wide-ranging interview on the Rugby Union Weekly podcast, O'Shea discussed:

England's prospects next year, with O'Shea believing England are one of five teams who can win the 2027 World Cup

the RFU's stringent selection rules for England players, with O'Shea saying the unintended consequences of picking players based overseas would be "massive"

the succession plan for Red Roses boss Mitchell and how O'Shea doesn't feel the England women's side can ever be too strong despite their four-year dominance of the world game.

Conor O'Shea: Borthwick's contract, overseas rule & Red Roses

Following a review into England's "horrendous" Six Nations earlier this year, Borthwick has been backed to lead the team through to the World Cup, with O'Shea adding he can't see a scenario where Borthwick isn't in charge in Australia.

In the July leg of the Nations Championship, England recovered from a bruising defeat by South Africa in Johannesburg to vanquish Fiji in Liverpool and edge out Argentina to finish the campaign with two wins from three.

However at this stage the RFU has stopped short of committing to Borthwick on a long-term basis, unlike Ireland, who have signed their head coach Andy Farrell up to 2031.

"I see in Steve someone who bleeds England, and wants England to succeed more than anything you can imagine," O'Shea said.

"This England team is unequivocally one of probably five teams who can win the World Cup next year. I believe this team can win a World Cup.

"Is the talent there? 100%," he added.

"If over this next 12 months this England team shows the best version of itself, I know it can beat anyone in the world."

As was the case for a number of his predecessors, Borthwick is only able to select players based in the English Prem, meaning the likes of Toulouse flanker Jack Willis – one of the outstanding performers in the French Top 14 – is ineligible for his country.

Cap centurion Courtney Lawes, who has returned to English rugby with Sale after two seasons at Brive, believes the RFU should review the policy to ensure the best players are available.

But O'Shea is adamant the ruling is what works for English rugby as a whole, and has warned against the impact of loosening the policy.

"It is something done not just for England, but for English rugby," O'Shea said.

"As of now, if all the best players were picked by England and went abroad, and we had less of the top players in our league, the unintended consequence towards investment into that from some of our owners… why would you invest in the pathways if the best players are going to be taken away?

"I get it completely, the life experiences are great. But for the English game, it is absolutely the right thing."

England should pick English-based players - Baxter

Allow overseas stars to play for England - Lawes

Since joining the RFU in January 2020, O'Shea has overseen England women's global dominance, aided by the establishment and development of Premiership Women's Rugby (PWR).

And while the resources and player numbers at England dwarf those at many of their rivals, O'Shea rejects the notion that the Red Roses can ever be too strong.

The world champion Roses are unbeaten in four years and have won every Six Nations since 2018.

Conversely in the men's game, no nation has won three Six Nations in a row in the professional era.

"Does competitive tension create greater commercialisation and broadcast? I get all that," O'Shea said.

"But I do think when you look at the PWR, and what we have done in terms of allowing a lot of players to come over here and allow them the platform to develop as players, England plays a huge role in driving that.

"Was it bad when you had a dominant Tiger Woods, or Serena Williams? What about celebrating what they are. They have been the standard bearer."

fullText:
The new model will serve as the first big test for John Ternus, who took the role last week

All eyes are on Apple’s annual fall announcement of new products this afternoon, where the company is expected to unveil the most significant change to the iPhone since the smartphone’s introduction in 2007.

Unlike previous iterations, the new iPhone is expected to fold, opening and closing like a passport to double its screen size.

The product release event, titled “Surprise and Shine”, begins at 10am Pacific Standard Time on Apple’s campus in Cupertino, California, south of San Francisco.

While competitors have released foldable smartphones since the late 2010s, the new model will be a first for the iPhone maker and will also serve as the first big test for the company’s new CEO, John Ternus, who assumed the role on 1 September.

Apple is expected to price the phone north of $2000, more than what some of its competitors charge for their foldable phones. A Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold, for instance, retails for $1899. Much remains unknown about Apple’s device, including its name, though it is rumored to be named either the iPhone Fold or the iPhone Ultra.

Apple reportedly began testing prototypes of its folding iPhone display in early 2021 – though at the time there were no plans for its launch, according to a Bloomberg report. Ultimately, the phone the company is rumored to launch will be about 5.5in when it’s closed and 7.8in when it opens. It’s also not expected to have Face ID because the device is too thin to hold the camera that would enable the facial recognition scan. Reports indicate it will only offer Touch ID instead.

Apple is also expected to make several more routine announcements, including new iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max models. Though the foldable iPhone may take center stage Wednesday, demand for foldable phones makes up only a small sliver of overall mobile device sales. Customers’ interest in standard iPhones, by contrast, remains high, as evidenced in Apple’s most recent robust earnings.

The company is also expected to unveil new iterations of some of its other product offerings at its events and over the next few months, including updates to its Apple Watch and AirPods lines, according to Bloomberg, as well as its first-ever touchscreen MacBook.

Ternus will take the stage as CEO for the first time and mark the beginning of his tenure as the head of Apple, replacing outgoing CEO Tim Cook. In a note to employees on his first day, Ternus said that he was excited about “the incredible products already in the works and the ones we haven’t even imagined”.

“I’m honored to be stepping into this role at what is truly the greatest company in the world, and I am so excited about everything we have in store,” Ternus wrote in his letter. “We have a huge launch next week that’s going to be phenomenal. Thanks for everything you’ve all done to make it possible.”

title: UK to force Apple and Google to block explicit images on children’s smartphones
description:
Lisa Nandy says government will introduce legislation after talks end without breakthrough
Apple and Google will be forced to block explicit images on children’s smartphones by law in the UK after talks failed to produce a breakthrough, the government has said.

fullText:
Lisa Nandy says government will introduce legislation after talks end without breakthrough

Apple and Google will be forced to block explicit images on children’s smartphones by law in the UK after talks failed to produce a breakthrough, the government has said.

The legislation commitment puts ministers on a collision course with two of the biggest players in Silicon Valley, months after the government announced a social media ban for under-16s.

Lisa Nandy, the secretary of state for digital, culture, media and sport, said the government would start work on an act of parliament to stop under-18s taking, sharing or viewing nude images on their devices.

Talks with Google and Apple, whose operating systems dominate the smartphone market, had not reached agreement as a three-month deadline passed on Tuesday.

Nandy told the House of Commons the tech companies could still reach a deal but it was “almost certain” groundbreaking legislation would be required.

“For too long, technology companies have failed to protect children from some of the worst harms,” she said. “And to be frank, I am not prepared to give them the benefit of the doubt that progress will continue at the pace that we need it to, while harm is being done now.”

The prime minister, Andy Burnham, said the protections would be “built into the device and switched on by default”, and tech companies will be required to verify an adult user’s age before they are allowed to take, view or send nude images. The government also wants the restrictions to apply to apps used by children, which will require further legislation.

Nandy said: “This will ensure that the whole ecosystem changes, tackling the means by which children are most often abused or groomed in the online world.”

Sources familiar with progress in the talks have said there iwas a desire to reach a deal on both sides but significant hurdles remained including privacy concerns on the tech side.

Jess Phillips, the Labour MP and former safeguarding minister, said the legislation would stop the UK from producing self-generated child sexual abuse material, where children are duped or groomed into sharing explicit images of themselves.

However, she urged the government to ensure the UK was followed by other countries and to make sure that “while we lead the world, we’re not standing alone for too long”.

Hannah Swirsky, head of policy at the Internet Watch Foundation, which monitors the online spread of child sexual abuse material [CSAM], said: “It is deeply disappointing that tech firms have failed to act in full, but we are pleased that the government is now taking decisive legislative action to keep children safe.”

Last year the IWF said a quarter of the images or videos of CSAM it recorded were self-generated, representing more than 140,000 pieces of content over a 12-month period.

One of Keir Starmer’s final acts as prime minister was to give Apple and Google three months to stop under-18s from generating, sending or seeing nude images on their devices, by activating built-in features on the hardware or other technological solutions. Between them, Apple’s iOS and Google’s Android smartphone operating systems dominate the mobile phone market.

The nudity block implies the use of “client-side scanning”, where content is scanned by software on the device before it is encrypted or sent.

“Client-side scanning is the least evil approach,” said Lukasz Olejnik, a visiting senior research fellow in cybersecurity and privacy at Kings College London. “That said, it does put in place an infrastructure to scan content of messages.”

Privacy campaigners have also warned that adults would have to verify their age before switching off any nudity-blocking features. In June, the government said the proposals would “not affect the use of devices owned and used by adults who verify their age”.

Google said it was “pleased to have made progress” in talks with the government and was “fully committed” to working with legislators, experts, app developers and device manufacturers to “keep children safe, while also protecting privacy and access to information”.

An Apple spokesperson said the company was preparing to strengthen its “communication safety” feature, which warns children when they are receiving or sending nude images and videos.

“We share the UK’s commitment to combating exploitation and abuse online, and have shared with UK officials future plans to strengthen communication safety and other tools even further to help keep kids safe.”

fullText:
Historically a new Grand Theft Auto game inspired controversy around violence – but this time people are getting exercised about its romance

There was never any doubt that Grand Theft Auto VI’s extended look would elicit a viral reaction from the internet. Having won the Game Awards’ Most Anticipated award twice consecutively, Rockstar’s forthcoming crime opus is one of the most frothed-over games in recent memory, or indeed ever. It’s nothing short of a cultural phenomenon.

One aspect of the game has provoked an unexpectedly vehement response on social media: not violence, but romance. Protagonists Lucia and Jason are in love, you see, and as a player, part of your job is keeping their spark alive and their relationship strong, so that their criminal escapades are underpinned by a strong connection to one another. Holding hands, enjoying a date at the beach, spontaneously texting one another when apart – all of these interactions will strengthen their bond. You’ll be putting in a lot of work to ensure this couple thrives, which is why some people have come to believe that playing GTA VI counts as micro-cheating.

Takes on this are all over social media. Multiple users have shared posts claiming that if you romance characters in video games such as GTA VI you’ve been unfaithful to your partner; TikTok account El Michelle remarked that simply playing the game is cheating. “In absolutely no human way is my fiance playing GTA VI,” posted Shelby Haas, another TikTok user. “You literally have to maintain a relationship with a girl […] you have to take her on dates, and you can have sex with her. […] Don’t let your boyfriend or fiance or husband play GTA 6.”

Over on TikTok, a post by Landry states that GTA VI “is basically the same as cheating”, continuing: “I guarantee you, if your man is playing GTA VI and keeping his little girlfriend alive on that video game, he’s most definitely the type that’s following models.”

GTA VI is by no means the inventor of in-game dating – hello, Baldur’s Gate 3, in which you can romance and have sex with any (or several) of your eight companions, including a druid who transforms into a bear. And surely we all remember trying to persuade our Sims to get off with each other. For at least 20 years dating and romance have been a significant element of all sorts of different titles; there is an entire (immensely popular) genre of dating games devoted to playfully living out virtual relationships.

Even so, due to its unrivalled online presence, GTA VI will be many people’s first exposure to the idea. Video game newcomers on TikTok seem especially exercised about the lengths their partners will go to to maintain a happy in-game relationship with Lucia, though it’s worth pointing out that it goes both ways: playing as Lucia, you’ll have to put just as much effort into maintaining a strong relationship with Jason. (The notion of maxing out the romance with Jason hasn’t provoked nearly as intense a response.)

It’s easy for people to revert to off-the-shelf misogynistic accusations about “jealous” and “overreactive” spouses in a situation like this, and indeed, many counter-commentators have done just that. “‘GTA VI is literally cheating’ is something I would say if I was a jealous, insecure hag […]” declares one TikToker. In the comments on one Instagram video, someone opined that GTA VI “promotes lust”, resulting in a massive pile-on.

But what if this isn’t knee-jerk jealousy? Behind these rather laughable concerns about virtual girlfriends, there are valid insecurities here over the idea of one’s real-life partner being more invested in a fictional character than a real-life relationship. Especially for young people, we’re in an age of loneliness and disconnection, fuelled by being chronically online. It’s one of the greatest paradoxes of modern society: despite being able to instantly engage with anyone or anything, these interactions are superficial and fleeting.

The dating scene right now is bleak. Dating columnist-cum-novelist Annie Lord believes the way we treat each other is part of the problem: “People treat each other as disposable because they’ve got the mindset of an app.” Factor in the growing influence of the manosphere, which many say has “ruined dating”, and it’s not hard to comprehend why experts say we’re experiencing a global dating crisis. Since 2014, the number of young people without close friendships/relationships has “risen fivefold”. Joke all you want about oversensitive gen Zs, but they are experiencing life in a social vacuum.

If you’re dealing in real life with men who don’t even text you back, let alone take you on a date, it’s easy to see why it would sting to watch them engage enthusiastically in a video-game relationship with a virtual woman whom they shower with expensive gifts, bouquets, and thoughtful messages. As TikToker RawTJR’s post joked: this is “how mfs gonna be treating Lucia in GTA 6 while treating their irl gf like shi”.

“I will NOT stand for people calling these partners ‘jealous’ or ‘overreacting’ when they clearly are trying to voice real concerns about their relationships,” wrote trans activist and sex educator Dee Whitnell in an Instagram post. “If someone feels underappreciated in their relationship but sees their partner fulfilling these needs for someone else (even if it is a game character), it’s totally understandable why they would feel a bit frustrated.”

As someone who explores every romance option in all games that allow it, I personally think it’s absurd to class in-game romances as a form of cheating – though I appreciate that individual boundaries can differ. People might more reasonably channel their concerns into conversations around AI companionship sites, such as Candy AI and DreamGF, that offer virtual sexbots. As far back as 2023 we were asking if an AI chatbot could be classed as cheating – and the technology has vastly improved since then.

More than anything else, this unexpected controversy around GTA VI highlights how dissatisfied and lonely many people are within their relationships. And a video game isn’t going to change that one way or another.

fullText:
Facilities likely to employ 10,400 workers, compared with 40,000 in industry estimates, thinktank says

Datacentres in the UK will create just a quarter of the jobs predicted by the tech sector, while consuming vast amounts of energy, according to new research.

Environmental thinktank Verdant predicts that all the datacentres currently planned are likely to directly employ 10,400 workers – compared with the more than 40,000 cited in projections by the industry lobby group TechUK.

Labour has defended the rapid rollout of AI datacentres in the face of growing public scepticism, amid concerns about their demand for water and energy. The government has also echoed TechUK’s claims about job creation.

Verdant’s analysis is based on 20 projects for which data on staffing levels are publicly available, including via planning applications, company accounts and press releases – as well as international comparisons.

It says the datacentres that have already been built have directly created fewer than 4,400 jobs – about 8.6 jobs for each megawatt of energy they consume, against the 43.7 jobs claimed in TechUK’s projections.

Verdant also argues that the many future projects currently at the planning stage are on a far larger scale, and so likely to be much less job-intensive – perhaps creating as few as 1.6 permanent positions per megawatt.

Its analysis focuses on the permanent workers needed to maintain and operate datacentres, setting aside the much larger number of temporary construction jobs needed to build them.

James Meadway, the thinktank’s co-director, said: “We’re being rushed into supporting a frantic pace of datacentre buildout on very flimsy economic grounds.

“Clearly artificial intelligence and related technologies have great potential. But vast new datacentres arrive at significant real costs to local communities and even our climate ambitions, and their use case has to be made by the government and industry – rather than assuming we can build first and then work out why we did later.”

To underline the resource intensity of the vast data warehouses, Verdant compared the 8.6 jobs they currently create per megawatt of power used with about 400 in a car plant and more than 3,600 in a hospital or health facility.

The government rejected this comparison, and questioned Verdant’s methodology. A spokesperson said: “This report relies on a deeply misleading jobs-per-megawatt metric, makes false comparisons with hospitals and schools, and appears to confuse electricity capacity with actual consumption. More seriously, it discounts the wider economic value of compute [computing capacity] and the national security and sovereignty case for building critical digital infrastructure in Britain.”

Verdant said it had based its calculations on the electricity capacity that tech firms claim they need – which could still crowd out alternative plans, even if the completed datacentres don’t end up using all the capacity.

Labour has classified AI datacentres as critical national infrastructure in an attempt to speed up the planning process, and Andy Burnham has underlined his backing for the sector by appointing AI minister Kanishka Narayan to his cabinet.

Narayan has advocated a rapid increase in datacentres, partly on grounds of national sovereignty. He told the Times last month: “The British public is very clear that it wants strong defence. It wants strong, sovereign capability, it doesn’t just want foreign billionaires to own things that matter to our lives. If we’re being true to those British values, it is impossible to achieve that without building a sovereign level of datacentre capacity in this country.”

Zack Polanski, the party’s leader in England, said: “The government is planning to steamroller local opposition so private companies can build datacentres – but it can’t explain what the benefits are.

‘“England and Wales are still facing drought after our hottest summer ever, but these datacentres are set to be given priority access to water. Meanwhile, this latest research suggests far fewer jobs may actually be created in constructing and staffing them than the government claims.”

In response to the Green party’s call for a “pause”, a government spokesperson insisted that it would “simply send investment and good jobs abroad, while leaving Britain dependent on overseas computing for the processing of sensitive health and defence data”.

A spokesperson for TechUK said: “Our estimates that the UK datacentre industry supports 43,500 jobs, and could support 40,000 more by 2035, are built on a published methodology using industry data and standard economic impact assessment techniques. The figures were built transparently from the best available industry data at the time, and we are confident they remain a reasonable estimate of the sector’s employment contribution.”

title: I'm a former Accenture consultant. I saw why so many workplace conflicts go unresolved.
description: At Accenture, Lauren Bronson saw senior leaders struggle to confront toxic clients. Now, she helps leaders find common ground.
fullText:
Lauren Bronson Petrous, a former Accenture consultant, is a conflict resolution specialist.

She spent two years at Accenture and has one takeaway: Consultants hate conflict.

She now helps teams with leadership development and conflict resolution.

This is a conversation with Lauren Bronson Petrous, a former senior consultant at Accenture, who now leads the advisory firm Boundless & Co. This conversation has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Conflict's inevitable. We're all going to have it. How is everyone so terrified of it?

That was the question that kept coming up during my time as a senior consultant at Accenture.

Throughout my career, I've worked with executives and senior leaders across industries, from media companies to international consulting firms. One pattern has become clear: Regardless of title, many leaders struggle to navigate difficult conversations and receive feedback — both essential to building a successful company where people want to work

At Accenture, I saw people leading teams on $10 million contracts who could not address difficult clients or colleagues. Sometimes I would sit in meetings with senior leaders where no one was really achieving anything because no one was willing to address the elephant in the room. Then there were those who were not afraid to say direct things, but did so without grace, timing, or care.

I joined Accenture after earning a master's degree in organizational change from Northwestern. One of my professors had pitched me to the firm without my knowing. I went through the interview process and got an offer, but I initially said no because I wanted to start my own gig. The firm told me they thought I could do phenomenal work, so I joined as a senior consultant.

Accenture is a machine. After onboarding and training, the firm identifies people based on their skill sets and determines which projects they should be on. It is partly about capacity — who is available — but also about who is most skilled for a particular client. You would meet with a client, and if they liked you and it worked well, you would start the project.

I often led teams. A lot of my work involved organizational change, team development, and leadership development.

Across my career, I've noticed that talented people do not necessarily have leadership skills. Many companies hire for talent and high performance, then put people into managerial or leadership roles without giving them the skills to lead. They are expected to handle conflict, develop their team, and be a boss people actually respect.

I left Accenture in December 2023 to start Boundless & Co., a coaching and consulting firm. I decided to leave because I wanted to help clients in a more tailored, customized way and address root issues such as navigating conflict, unresolved tension, and avoidance that often stunt company culture and momentum.

Now, about half of my work is leadership-development coaching, and about half is helping companies resolve conflict. I often work with cofounders or senior leaders who are considering dismantling a $10 million or $50 million company because they cannot agree on how to lead it.

Resolution does not mean we are all holding hands and becoming best friends. It means both people can walk away with clarity about how to move forward.

title: Remains found 49 years ago in North Carolina identified as teen runaway
description: Skeletal remains found in North Carolina in 1977 have been identified as those of Cindy Marcell Blizzard, a 15-year-old girl who ran away from her home in Monkton, Maryland, investigators said.
fullText:
Nearly half a century after a set of skeletal remains were found in a wooded part of North Carolina, they have been identified as those of a 15-year-old runaway who vanished in 1977.

The remains were found on Dec. 29, 1977, in a wooded area near a manufacturing plant in Wilson County, North Carolina. Investigators determined that the remains had likely been there for between six months and two years, according to a news release from the North Carolina State Bureau of Investigation. They were determined to likely belong to a White female between 16 and 23.

Investigators have treated the case as a homicide because of the circumstances surrounding the discovery of the remains. But no suspects were ever determined, and the identity of the remains could not be confirmed. Police used dental records but were unable to find a match, the bureau said. Eventually, the case went cold.

In 2010, a state anthropologist reopened the case and submitted the teeth for DNA testing. The resulting DNA profiles were entered into national databases, but no matches were found, according to investigators.

In 2024, the case was reviewed by a special investigator from the bureau's Cold Case Investigative Team. The investigator, Andy Murr, sent a bone sample to a forensic DNA lab that extracted genetic material to build a complex profile. That profile was used to trace potential relatives.

That pointed Murr and other investigators to the case of Cindy Marcell Blizzard, a 15-year-old girl who ran away from her home in Monkton, Maryland, in the spring of 1977.

The genetic information and efforts from local, state and federal agencies allowed investigators to confirm the remains as belonging to Blizzard. A photo of Blizzard shared by investigators shows a young woman with light hair and blue eyes. Other information about her life and family was not shared by the bureau.

The investigation into Blizzard's death remains ongoing. Anyone with information about Blizzard is asked to call the North Carolina State Bureau of Investigation's Cold Case Tip Line, email the agency or contact the Wilson County Sheriff's Office.

NAGOYA, Japan (AP) — Athletes who've arrived early for the Asian Games were unharmed by extensive flooding that hit the central Japanese city of Nagoya, Mayor Ichiro Hirosawa said Wednesday.

"We are not worried about the conditions of the venues and we believe there is no problem holding the Asian Games as planned," Hirosawa told reporters.

The Asian Games, an event with more athletes than the Summer Olympics, open Sept. 19 in Nagoya and surrounding areas and run through Oct. 4.

More than 11,000 athletes are signed up from 45 countries and regions in Asia. By comparison, about 10,700 athletes participated in the Summer Olympics in 2024 in Paris.

The previous edition of the Asian Games was held three years ago in Hangzhou, China.

Hirosawa said about 400 athletes and staff who are staying in converted shipping containers — remodeled to serve as temporary housing units for the Asian Games — were briefly evacuated to higher ground during the heavy rain.

He said there were a number of leaking roofs but nothing more serious around the dozens of Games venues.

Record rain fell in parts of the city on Tuesday, flooding dozens of roads and homes, and stranding pedestrians and vehicles. City bus and subway operations were temporarily suspended, the mayor said.

Reports said about 3,500 people took shelter at emergency evacuation centers.

title: Netanyahu faces backlash over report he was warned of Hamas attack days before October 7
description: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu faced a fierce political backlash Tuesday over a report that the president of the UAE had warned him of a major Hamas operation days before the October 7, 202...
fullText:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu faced a fierce political backlash Tuesday over a report that the president of the UAE had warned him of a major Hamas operation days before the October 7, 2023 attack.

The Prime Minister's Office dismissed the report as an "absolute lie." But with Israel's October elections less than two months away, Netanyahu's rivals seized on it as the latest evidence of what they say is a growing list of warnings he had ignored.

The four opposition party leaders – Gadi Eisenkot, Naftali Bennett, Avigdor Lieberman and Yair Golan – issued a rare joint statement calling for "an immediate and thorough investigation" into Netanyahu's "failures and malfunctioning."

"The Israeli public is entitled to know: What did Netanyahu know, when did he know, why he didn't update the security establishment, and why he didn't act to protect Israeli civilians?" the statement said.

Former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett said the report is "true," writing on X that Netanyahu's alleged disregard for the warnings amounts to "criminal negligence." Bennett's political ally, former Prime Minister Yair Lapid, said he too had publicly warned of an attack before it happened, as had top Israeli security officials as well as Egyptian officials. "If Netanyahu had fulfilled his role, the massacre would have been prevented," Lapid said in a statement.

The report, published in the Haaretz newspaper, was based on findings from an upcoming book by Israeli journalists Shlomi Eldar and Ruti Yuval. It said UAE President Sheikh Mohammed bin Zayed called Netanyahu about 10 days before October 7 and, during a 45-minute call, warned him that Hamas' Gaza leader Yahya Sinwar was planning a major move against Israel that could cause bloodshed and destabilize the region. The report cited a message Sinwar conveyed to the UAE and Israel through a Palestinian mediator in mid-September 2023, warning of an upcoming "earthquake."

Haaretz reported that Netanyahu reacted "relatively calmly" to the information, and assured Bin Zayed that Israel was prepared for any scenario.

The UAE's Foreign Ministry issued a statement on Tuesday evening saying that it "does not comment on media stories or speculation regarding conversations between government leaders" but did not deny the call. "When necessary, all relevant intelligence has been and continues to be communicated between the relevant entities," the statement said.

An Israeli source familiar with the matter said Netanyahu's office had tried to get the UAE to deny the Haaretz report, but the UAE only agreed to put out a statement about intelligence sharing.

The Prime Minister's Office strongly denied the report, stating Netanyahu "did not speak with the president of the United Arab Emirates during the period in question and did not receive any warning from him."

Eldar, one of the journalists behind the report, pushed back on Netanyahu's denial of the report.

"It's true," he told CNN's Jake Tapper. "I worked on this report for almost a year and a half," he said.

"I have the document, I have records, I have everything that shows that the president of the UAE called Netanyahu a week an a half before October 7 and gave him a warning that Yahya Sinwar is planning a major attack on Israel," Eldar said.

The report comes as Netanyahu's rivals work to make accountability for October 7 – the deadliest attack in Israel's history, during which over 1,200 people were murdered and more than 250 abducted to Gaza – a central campaign issue.

Netanyahu has now outlasted nearly every member of Israel's top security leadership from that day. Since the attack, the defense minister, the military chief of staff, and the directors of military intelligence, the Mossad and the Shin Bet, have all either resigned, been ousted, or reached the end of their terms.

Gadi Eisenkot, currently polling as Netanyahu's leading challenger, said the Haaretz report shows Netanyahu "led Israel blindly" toward the October 7 failures and renewed his pledge to establish a state commission of inquiry if elected.

Nearly three years after the attack, Netanyahu has resisted demands from bereaved families and October 7 survivors to establish an independent commission to investigate the security and intelligence failures that enabled Hamas to conduct the operation.

He and his associates have instead promoted a narrative blaming security chiefs for not waking him up the night before the attack despite intelligence indications that a Hamas offensive was imminent.

Last month, his wife, Sara Netanyahu, suggested that Yair Golan – a retired major general and the leader of the left-wing Democrats party who independently rushed to the Gaza border on October 7 to rescue survivors – had advance knowledge of the attack.

In an interview with the pro-government Channel 14, she questioned how Golan was "already dressed and ready" at dawn that day to head south, "while others knew nothing, including the prime minister."

Golan demanded an apology for what he called a "vile conspiracy theory" and said he would pursue a defamation suit, calling the allegation part of Netanyahu's attempt to "rewrite" the events of October 7 and deflect responsibility.

Following the Haaretz report, Golan wrote on X that the prime minister's "they-didn't-wake-me-up narrative is over. He knew, he was warned." He called it "not an error in judgment, but a conscious and criminal abandonment."

Hours later, the Democrats party sharpened its electoral campaign against Netanyahu, erecting a giant billboard over Tel Aviv's main highway bearing the headline: "The 1,200 murdered file – Causing death by negligence."

title: Incumbent GOP governor rolls to primary victory after keeping Trump at a distance

First-term Republican Governor Kelly Ayotte easily handled her primary opponents Tuesday, setting up a high-stakes general election battle against Democratic gubernatorial nominee Cinde Warmington, who ran unopposed for her party's nomination.

Ayotte defeated Republican challengers Shaun Fife and Bob Wayne McClory as she seeks a second two-year term leading the Granite State.

The former senator and state Attorney General entered Tuesday's primary as the incumbent after winning the governor's mansion in 2024, when Ayotte defeated former Manchester Mayor Joyce Craig and kept the office in Republican hands following the retirement of four-term GOP Gov. Chris Sununu.

Ayotte previously served as New Hampshire's attorney general from 2004 to 2009 before winning election to the U.S. Senate in 2010. She served one term before narrowly losing her 2016 reelection campaign to Democrat Maggie Hassan.

In 2024, following Sununu's decision not to seek a fifth two-year term, Ayotte mounted a political comeback with the outgoing governor's endorsement.

In her first term, Ayotte successfully pushed to roll back portions of the state's bail reform law, arguing the existing system was too lenient on criminal suspects awaiting trial, signed legislation requiring public schools to restrict student cellphone use and pushed penalties for motorists who refuse Breathalyzer tests.

Tuesday marked her second campaign for governor after Warmington lost the 2024 Democratic gubernatorial primary.

Warmington has attacked Ayotte for failing to adequately stand up to President Donald Trump, citing healthcare cuts, tariffs and the war in Iran.

title: I lost $180,000 in Wall Street retirement savings. Now, I drive Uber and Lyft 75 hours a week.
description: Bill Lewis, a former Wall Street broker, now drives for Uber and Lyft after losing his retirement savings in a failed franchise venture.
fullText:
Bill Lewis worked on Wall Street for more than 20 years but was laid off in 2013.

After the layoff, he went into business for himself and invested his 401(k) into a franchise.

The franchise failed after four years, and he's been driving for Uber and Lyft ever since.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Bill Lewis, 58, an Uber and Lyft driver who lives in the Poconos and has completed about 43,000 trips. He previously worked on Wall Street and owned a Nestlé Toll House franchise. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

I'm 58 and working harder than I ever have. I drive for Uber and Lyft seven days a week, about 75 hours in total.

I didn't expect to be in this position.

I once had about $180,000 in my 401(k), built over a career that included more than two decades on Wall Street.

I started as a runner at the American Stock Exchange in 1989, eventually became a broker, and was laid off in 2013 as algorithms reduced the need for people on the trading floor.

After Wall Street, I decided to try something completely different and go into business for myself.

I put all of that retirement money into a Nestlé Toll House franchise, a retail dessert bakery chain. I didn't know how to run a business and thought buying a franchise would help because I could rely on the company's structure.

The sales weren't the problem. In my first year, the franchise saw strong sales growth compared with the year before. However, it felt like the mall was simply too expensive for me to turn a profit.

I ran the business for four years. By the end, I had made less from those four years than the $7 I earned on my first Uber ride.

I make about $75,000 a year driving for Uber and Lyft. The main thing keeping me in gig work is the freedom.

If something happens at home, I can stop driving. If my brakes need repairs, I don't have to call a boss. I've always liked driving, and I've learned how to earn a living doing it.

Still, I know how quickly things can change.

I definitely regret putting my retirement savings into the Nestlé Toll House franchise. That decision is the reason I'm working harder than ever now.

If I hadn't put the money into the business, I'd probably still have my retirement fund and be a lot better off.

So for now, I keep driving. There are parts of the work I value and parts that frustrate me. The biggest is the way Uber treats drivers.

I started driving for Uber in 2017, and I've learned that making a living at this means being selective.

Uber gives me about eight to 10 seconds to look at a ride and calculate what I'd make per hour, consider the mileage and return trip, and decide whether it's worth taking.

That's part of my frustration with Uber.

I understand that Uber is a business and needs to make money. I worked on Wall Street, so I'm not against big business. I just want drivers to be treated fairly.

It's frustrating when it feels like the company has all the information, while I have seconds to figure out whether a ride makes financial sense for my bottom line.

I've seen offers of around $80 to drive 75 miles to Brooklyn, for example. Once I factor in the return trip, gas, and about $25 in tolls, I could actually lose money by accepting that trip. That's why I haven't taken an Uber trip into New York City in five years.

I've gotten better at protecting my bottom line by taking only rides that meet my $30-an-hour target and using Lyft more often.

Lyft shows me an estimated hourly rate for each ride, which makes it easier to quickly identify offers that meet my target.

Since becoming more selective about the Uber rides I choose and taking more Lyft rides, I've increased my pay by almost 25% since earlier this year.

An Uber spokesperson told Business Insider, "We're committed to making Uber the best platform for drivers and regularly engage with them on their experience. Drivers have full control over whether to accept or decline any offer that's made to them. Where Upfront Fares are live, drivers see key details before accepting a trip, including exactly how much they'll earn and the rider's destination, so they can decide whether a trip works for them."
